abortcontroller.d: Standard way to cancel async work: pass signal to fetch, then call controller.abort(), or use AbortSignal.timeout(ms) for a deadline. The request rejects with AbortError or TimeoutError.

abtest.d: A randomized experiment comparing a control and a variant on a metric. Pre-decide the metric, sample size and duration; avoid peeking; check sample ratio mismatch; correct for multiple metrics; and watch guardrail metrics. Statistical power sets the needed sample size.

accesstier.d: Blob pricing tiers (Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive) that trade lower storage cost for higher access cost.

accesstoken.d: A short-lived JWT proving who the user is, sent with each API request.

accountvending.d: An automated pipeline that creates a new cloud account or subscription with the baseline already applied: logging, security agents, network attachment, budgets, tags and access. It turns days of tickets into minutes.

acid.d: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the guarantees a transactional database provides.

acme.d: The protocol (used by Let's Encrypt and others) that issues and renews TLS certificates automatically. Certificate lifetimes are being shortened on a published schedule, so automated renewal and expiry monitoring are mandatory.

acr.d: Azure's private registry for container images, accessible by managed identity.

actionspin.d: Referencing a GitHub Action or image by its full immutable commit or digest instead of a movable tag, so a hijacked tag cannot change what runs. Use Dependabot or Renovate to update pins.

activation.d: The non-linear function applied to a neuron's weighted sum. Without it, stacked layers collapse into one linear function. Sigmoid and tanh squash values; ReLU outputs max(0, x) and is the common default.

adamw.d: The default optimizer for transformers: Adam's per-parameter adaptive step sizes with weight decay applied directly to the weights instead of through the gradient. Usually paired with learning-rate warmup, cosine decay and gradient clipping.

adapterpattern.d: A wrapper that translates a library or service interface into the one your code wants. Your core depends on a PaymentGateway interface and a StripeAdapter implements it, so a vendor change touches one file.

aesgcm.d: A mode of the AES cipher that encrypts and authenticates in one step, so tampered ciphertext fails to decrypt. Each message needs a unique IV (nonce) under the same key.

agent.d: A model running in a loop that chooses tools, observes results and decides next steps until a task is done.

agentcheckpoint.d: Saving the transcript and state after each step so a crashed, paused or approval-waiting agent run can resume where it stopped instead of restarting. Also the basis for replaying a run during debugging.

agentloop.d: The cycle of model response, tool execution and result feedback that repeats until the model gives a final answer.

aggregate.d: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX collapse many rows into one value, usually with GROUP BY. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) skips NULLs.

aiosemaphore.d: A primitive that lets at most N coroutines into a section at once. Used to bound concurrent HTTP calls or database work.

airflow.d: A workflow orchestrator where pipelines are DAGs (directed acyclic graphs) of tasks with schedules, retries, alerts and backfills. It should trigger and monitor work, not run heavy computation itself. Dagster and Prefect are common alternatives.

alb.d: An AWS layer-7 load balancer that routes HTTP and HTTPS requests to targets such as ECS tasks.

alertfatigue.d: When too many noisy or unactionable alerts cause on-call engineers to ignore or slow-walk real incidents. Page only on urgent, actionable user impact.

algconfusion.d: A class of JWT bugs where the verifier trusts the token's own alg header, accepting unsigned tokens or verifying an RS256 token as HS256 with the public key. Prevent it by pinning the expected algorithm.

algobias.d: Systematic unfairness from biased or unrepresentative data, proxy variables, mismatched objectives (such as cost for need), feedback loops and deployment context. Removing a sensitive column rarely helps because proxies reconstruct it.

allowlist.d: Accept only values you explicitly list (hosts, file extensions, column names, URL schemes) instead of trying to block bad ones. Blocklists are bypassed by encodings and variants; allow-lists fail closed.

analyzer.d: The pipeline that turns text into index terms: a tokenizer splits words, then filters lowercase, remove stop words, stem (running to run), apply synonyms or build edge n-grams for autocomplete. Index and query time analysis must match; inspect with the _analyze API.

ann.d: Finding vectors that are probably the closest to a query without comparing against every stored vector, using an index such as HNSW or IVF. It trades a small, measurable loss of recall for large gains in speed, so measure ANN recall against exact search on your own data.

anonrole.d: Postgres roles Supabase uses: anon for signed-out requests and authenticated for signed-in users.

ansible.d: An agentless automation tool that configures machines over SSH using YAML playbooks and idempotent modules. It is push-based and typically used for operating system, package, file and service configuration and orchestration.

ansiblecollection.d: A distributable package of modules, plugins and roles, installed with ansible-galaxy and referenced by fully qualified names such as ansible.builtin.copy or amazon.aws.aws_ec2. Pin collection versions in requirements.yml.

ansiblerole.d: A reusable directory layout bundling tasks, defaults, handlers, templates and files for one concern such as nginx. Role defaults are the lowest-precedence variables so callers can override them.

ansiblevault.d: Built-in encryption for variable files and individual strings in an Ansible project. For shared secrets a lookup against a secrets manager keeps values out of Git, and no_log keeps them out of run output.

apikeyhygiene.d: Keep keys in environment variables or a secrets manager, never in code, front ends or logs; call the API from your server; rotate keys and set budgets. A key pushed to a public repository is scraped within minutes.

apiversioning.d: The policy for evolving an API without breaking clients: additive changes in place, breaking changes behind a new version (path, header or date pin), with deprecation notice and the Sunset header.

appgateway.d: Azure's regional layer-7 load balancer with an optional web application firewall.

appmeta.d: Auth metadata fields. app_metadata is server-controlled and safe for roles; user_metadata can be edited by the user, so never use it for authorization.

appofapps.d: A parent Argo CD Application whose manifests are themselves Applications, used to bootstrap a whole cluster from one root. ApplicationSets are often easier to maintain for many similar apps, and wave health gating should be tested before you rely on it.

approuter.d: The Next.js routing system based on the app directory, using layouts, Server Components and streaming.

appservice.d: Azure's managed hosting for web apps and APIs, with deployment slots and built-in scaling.

appset.d: An Argo CD resource that generates many Applications from one template using generators such as git directories, cluster lists, pull requests or matrices. Common for one app per environment, cluster or preview.

argoapp.d: The Argo CD custom resource that maps a path in a Git repository, or a Helm chart, to a destination cluster and namespace, with a sync policy such as automated prune and selfHeal.

argon2.d: The recommended password hashing algorithm: deliberately slow and memory-hard so GPU cracking is expensive. OWASP's minimum settings are 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations and 1 lane.

argorollouts.d: A controller that adds a Rollout resource with canary and blue-green strategies, traffic weighting and metric analysis with automatic abort. Flagger fills a similar role in the Flux ecosystem.

argparse.d: The standard module that parses command-line arguments into typed options with automatic --help and error messages. Pass an explicit list to parse_args in tests instead of relying on sys.argv.

arima.d: Classical models that forecast from past values (autoregression), past errors (moving average) and differencing to remove trend; SARIMA adds seasonal terms and SARIMAX adds external regressors. They suit single series with modest history, and statsmodels implements them.

arn.d: The unique identifier for an AWS resource, such as arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket.

arrangeactassert.d: The shape of a clear test: set up the situation, do the one thing under test, check the outcome. Small, independent, fast tests whose names describe behaviour and that fail for exactly one reason.

asgi.d: Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface: the standard between async Python web servers (uvicorn, Hypercorn) and frameworks (FastAPI, Starlette). It supports HTTP, WebSockets and streaming.

aspnetcore.d: Microsoft's open-source web framework for .NET: a middleware pipeline plus built-in dependency injection, configuration, authentication, rate limiting, health checks and OpenAPI. Controllers and minimal APIs run on the same pipeline.

assertion.d: A statement of something that must be true; the program stops with a message if not, turning a wrong answer later into a precise failure now. Use for programming errors, not user input (Python drops asserts under -O).

asvs.d: OWASP's detailed list of security requirements you can test an application against, organized in levels of rigor. Teams use it as the requirement list behind the Top 10.

asyncawait.d: An async function always returns a promise; await pauses that function until a promise settles and gives the value or throws the rejection, so ordinary try/catch/finally works. The rest of the program keeps running.

asyncforeach.d: forEach ignores the promises its callback returns, so code after it runs before the work finishes. Use for...of with await (sequential) or await Promise.all(items.map(async ...)) (concurrent).

asyncio.d: Python's standard-library framework for single-threaded concurrency: an event loop plus tasks, queues, timeouts and non-blocking I/O primitives.

asynctask.d: A coroutine scheduled on the event loop so it runs concurrently with its creator. Keep a reference to it, because the loop holds only a weak one.

atleastonce.d: A delivery guarantee where every event is delivered one or more times, so duplicates and reordering are expected. Receivers must deduplicate and be idempotent.

attention.d: The mechanism that lets each token weigh every other token in the context to decide what is relevant.

aurora.d: AWS's cloud-built relational engine compatible with PostgreSQL and MySQL, with auto-growing storage and fast failover.

authcode.d: The standard OAuth flow for user sign-in: the browser is redirected to the identity provider, returns with a short-lived code, and your server exchanges the code for tokens. Always combine it with PKCE.

authuid.d: A Supabase helper that returns the signed-in user's id from the JWT. Write it as (select auth.uid()) in policies so it runs once per query.

autograd.d: PyTorch's automatic differentiation: operations on tensors that require gradients are recorded in a graph, and loss.backward() walks it in reverse to fill each parameter's .grad. Gradients accumulate, so call zero_grad each step.

availabilityzone.d: One or more data centers in a Region with independent power and networking. Spreading across zones survives a data center failure.

awsorganizations.d: The AWS service that groups accounts into a hierarchy of organizational units under a management account, with consolidated billing and policies such as SCPs attached at the root, OU or account.

azfunctions.d: Azure's function-as-a-service for event-driven code; new apps should use the Flex Consumption plan.

azmonitor.d: Azure's monitoring platform for metrics, logs and traces, including application performance data.

azpolicy.d: An Azure service that enforces organizational rules on resources, such as allowed regions or required tags.

azrbac.d: Azure's authorization system: role assignments grant a principal a role at a scope, inherited downward.

azsub.d: A billing and limits boundary in Azure that contains resource groups and resources.

backfill.d: Re-running a pipeline over past dates, for example after fixing a bug. It only works if jobs take a logical date as input (not the current time) and are idempotent, so a rerun of March reproduces March exactly.

backoffjitter.d: Retrying after waits that grow exponentially (0.1s, 0.2s, 0.4s) with a random component so clients do not retry in lockstep. Only retry idempotent operations, cap attempts, and add a retry budget, or a slowdown becomes a retry storm.

backpressure.d: A signal that a consumer cannot keep up, so the producer should pause until it can accept more data.

backprop.d: Computes the gradient of the loss for every weight with one backward sweep, applying the chain rule layer by layer and reusing stored forward values. Frameworks automate it as autograd.

backtesting.d: Evaluating a forecaster by repeatedly training on data up to a cutoff and testing on the period after it, moving the cutoff forward (expanding or sliding window). It respects time order, unlike random k-fold, and shows how error varies across periods.

backtracking.d: Depth-first search over choices with pruning: build a candidate step by step and abandon a branch as soon as it cannot lead to a solution. Used for permutations, subsets, N-queens, sudoku and constraint problems; worst case is exponential.

baselinemodel.d: A simple reference model, such as always predicting the majority class, that any real model must beat.

bastion.d: An Azure service for browser-based SSH or RDP to virtual machines that have no public IP address.

bayes.d: P(A|B) = P(B|A) x P(A) / P(B): update a prior belief with evidence. The key lesson is base-rate neglect: a 99% accurate test for a 1-in-1,000 event gives mostly false alarms, which is why precision depends on prevalence.

behavioraltest.d: Tests that assert properties a model must satisfy, such as invariance to irrelevant changes or a monotonic response to a feature, on fixed example rows. They catch absurd behavior that aggregate metrics hide.

bigkey.d: A big key is a single huge hash, list or set that makes deleting or fetching it block Redis for a long time; a hot key is one key receiving disproportionate traffic and saturating a single shard. Split big structures, use UNLINK and SCAN-family commands, and cache hot values locally.

bigo.d: Describes how an algorithm's time or memory grows with input size n, ignoring constants: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2).

binarysearch.d: Finds a value in a sorted array in O(log n) by repeatedly halving the search range; the idea behind ordered indexes.

bisect.d: Binary search through history for the commit that introduced a bug: mark a good and a bad commit, test the midpoint Git checks out, and repeat. With git bisect run and a test script it finds the culprit among 1,000 commits in about 10 steps.

bisectdebug.d: Cut the search space in half and test which half holds the bug, then repeat: about ten tests for 1,000 rows. Works on data, code, configuration and, with git bisect, commits.

blastradius.d: How much can break if a change or credential goes wrong. In IaC you limit it by splitting state per environment and layer (network, data, apps), scoping apply roles tightly, and protecting critical resources with prevent_destroy.

blockloop.d: Running slow synchronous work (time.sleep, requests, CPU loops, sync DB drivers) inside async code, which freezes every other task on that loop until it returns.

bluegreen.d: Running the old (blue) and new (green) versions side by side, then switching traffic at once. Rollback is switching back, at the cost of double capacity during the release.

bm25.d: A classic keyword ranking function that scores documents by term frequency and rarity; the standard for keyword search.

bodyparser.d: Middleware that reads the request stream, checks Content-Type, parses JSON or form data and sets req.body. Must be registered before the routes that read it; in Express 5 req.body is undefined if no parser ran.

booleanmask.d: A True/False array used to select elements or rows (df.loc[df['qty'] > 1]). Masking returns a copy; slices of arrays are views that change the original.

boolquery.d: The Query DSL's way of combining clauses: must (required, scored), should (optional boost), filter (required, not scored, cacheable) and must_not. Put yes/no conditions such as category or price range in filter context for speed.

boxmodel.d: Every element is a box: content, padding, border, margin. box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border, which is why most stylesheets set it globally.

branchprediction.d: CPUs overlap instructions in a pipeline and guess which way each if will go; a wrong guess costs on the order of 10 to 20 cycles. Out-of-order execution and SIMD (one instruction on many values) add speed, which is why predictable branches and vectorized code run faster.

branchprotection.d: Repository rules on key branches: required reviews, required passing checks, no force pushes. They stop a single mistake or compromised account from changing production code unreviewed.

brandedtype.d: A pattern that intersects a primitive with a phantom tag (string & { __brand: 'UserId' }) so IDs of different kinds cannot be mixed up. It is erased at runtime.

breakglass.d: A pair of highly privileged emergency identities with hardware MFA and offline credentials, used only when normal SSO or identity systems fail. Any use should trigger an alert.

breakpoint.d: A debugger pauses the program at a chosen line so you can inspect variables and step line by line. In Python call breakpoint() or run python -m pdb; IDEs and browser DevTools offer the same.

brin.d: A tiny index that stores min and max per block range; works for huge tables whose data is naturally ordered.

broadcast.d: Realtime feature for sending low-latency messages between connected clients without touching the database.

btree.d: A balanced tree of sorted pages; the default index type in Postgres, good for equality, ranges and sorting.

bucket.d: A named container for files in Supabase Storage. Access is governed by policies on storage.objects.

buf.d: A toolchain for protobuf that lints schemas, generates code and detects breaking changes against a previous version, so contract mistakes are caught in CI.

buffer.d: A fixed-size chunk of raw bytes in memory, used for binary data in Node.js.

bullmq.d: A Node.js job queue built on Redis with delayed and repeatable jobs, retries with backoff, concurrency control, rate limiting and parent-child flows. Workers need a Redis connection with maxRetriesPerRequest set to null. Sidekiq is the Ruby counterpart.

bundler.d: A build tool (Vite, webpack, esbuild, Rollup, Turbopack) that compiles TypeScript and JSX, resolves imports, tree-shakes, minifies and splits code into fingerprinted files for the browser.

burnrate.d: How fast the error budget is being consumed compared with plan. Alerting on burn rate over paired long and short windows catches both fast outages and slow leaks.

bypassrls.d: A Postgres role attribute that skips Row Level Security entirely. The service_role has it.

cacheaside.d: The common caching pattern: the application reads the cache, on a miss loads from the database and fills the cache, and on a write updates the database then deletes the cached key. Simple and resilient; the cache can be lost without losing data.

cachebreakpoint.d: A marker (the cache_control field in Anthropic's API) showing where the reusable prefix of a prompt ends. Everything before it, in the order tools, system, messages, can be served from the prompt cache if it is byte-identical on the next call; one changed character before the marker causes a miss.

cachecontrol.d: HTTP caching headers: max-age sets freshness, no-cache forces revalidation, no-store forbids storing, private limits to the browser. An ETag lets the client revalidate with If-None-Match and get a body-less 304. Fingerprint static assets and cache them for a year.

cachelocality.d: CPUs move memory in cache lines (typically 64 bytes) and bet that you reuse nearby and recent data. Sequential access over contiguous arrays is far faster than pointer chasing or strided access; false sharing between cores can ruin parallel scaling.

cachestampede.d: When a hot cache entry expires and many requests miss at once, all recomputing it and flattening the database. Defenses: request coalescing (one recompute, others wait), jittered TTLs, and serving stale data while refreshing in the background.

cachettl.d: How long a cached prompt prefix stays available. Anthropic documents a 5-minute default (refreshed on each read) and a 1-hour option; writes cost 1.25x (5 min) or 2x (1 h) the base input price and reads 0.1x. Choose the TTL from the gaps between your calls, since a gap longer than the TTL makes every call pay the write premium.

calibration.d: Making predicted probabilities match observed frequencies, so cases scored 0.7 really happen about 70 percent of the time. Fix with isotonic or sigmoid calibration and measure with the Brier score or a reliability curve.

callback.d: A function passed to another function to be called when work finishes. Node's convention is error-first: callback(err, result). Dependent steps nest deeper with every level.

callbackhell.d: Deeply nested callbacks, one level per dependent step, each repeating its own error check. Promises and async/await flatten the same flow into a straight line.

callstack.d: The memory region that records active function calls and their local variables. Unbounded recursion exhausts it and causes a stack overflow.

canary.d: Releasing a new version to a small share of traffic first and expanding only if metrics stay healthy.

cancellederror.d: The BaseException raised inside a coroutine at its current await when its task is cancelled. Clean up in finally and re-raise it; swallowing it breaks timeouts and TaskGroup.

candidategen.d: The first stage of a recommender or search system: cheaply narrow millions of items to hundreds or thousands using several sources (popularity, collaborative filtering, two-tower ANN, rules). A heavier ranking model then scores only those candidates.

captheorem.d: During a network partition, a replicated store must choose between consistency (refuse some requests rather than return stale or conflicting data) and availability (answer everyone, possibly with stale data). PACELC extends it: with no partition you still trade latency against consistency.

cardinality.d: The number of distinct values in a column, or how rows relate to each other (one-to-many).

catastrophicforgetting.d: A fine-tuned model losing general abilities it had before because its weights moved toward the narrow new data. Lower learning rates, fewer epochs, LoRA adapters and mixing in general data reduce it; a regression suite of general tasks detects it.

catboost.d: A gradient boosting library from Yandex with ordered boosting and ordered target statistics that reduce leakage when encoding categorical features, and strong defaults that often need little tuning.

catencoding.d: Converting categories to numbers. One-hot makes a column per value (fine for few categories); target encoding replaces a category with a label statistic and must be computed out-of-fold to avoid leakage; tree libraries like LightGBM and CatBoost can handle categories natively.

cd.d: Keeping the main branch always releasable and automating release steps. Continuous deployment goes further by shipping every green merge to production automatically.

cdc.d: Reading a database's write-ahead log to stream every insert, update and delete to other systems with low latency and without heavy queries. Debezium is the common open-source tool; plan for the initial snapshot and for schema changes.

cdn.d: A network of servers around the world that caches and serves content from a location close to each user.

celery.d: The standard Python distributed task queue: decorated functions run by workers, with brokers such as Redis, RabbitMQ or SQS, retries with backoff, Celery beat schedules and workflow primitives. Use acks_late and idempotent tasks, and mind the broker's visibility timeout.

cgroups.d: The Linux kernel features behind containers: namespaces give a process its own view of PIDs, network, mounts and users; cgroups limit and account CPU, memory and I/O. Containers share the host kernel, unlike virtual machines.

championchallenger.d: A release pattern where the serving model is the champion and a new candidate is the challenger, evaluated offline, in shadow mode or on a canary slice before it replaces the champion. Rollback means pointing back at the previous champion.

chaoseng.d: Deliberately injecting failures, such as killing instances or adding latency, in a controlled way to learn whether alerts, failover and runbooks really work.

chattemplate.d: The exact text format (special tokens and role markers) a chat model expects around system, user and assistant messages, stored with its tokenizer. Training or serving with a different template than the model was tuned on is a leading cause of degraded fine-tunes.

checkmode.d: ansible-playbook --check predicts changes without making them and --diff shows file differences. A scheduled check run against production doubles as drift detection.

cherrypick.d: Copying a single commit from one branch onto another as a new commit (git cherry-pick sha). Common for backporting a fix to a release branch; overuse creates duplicate history that is hard to reconcile.

chunking.d: Splitting documents into passages for indexing; good chunks are self-contained and a few hundred tokens long.

chunkoverlap.d: Repeating a small amount of text (a sentence or a few tokens) at the boundary between adjacent chunks so a fact that straddles a split survives intact in at least one chunk. The cost is duplicate content, so dedupe before prompting.

ci.d: Automatically building and testing every push so breakage is found within minutes. A good pipeline is fast (about ten minutes), reliable and required before merge.

cidr.d: Notation like 10.0.0.0/16 that fixes the network prefix length of an IP range; the remaining bits are host addresses (a /16 has 65,536).

circuitbreaker.d: A resilience pattern that stops calling a failing dependency: closed (normal), open (fail fast after repeated errors), half-open (probe occasionally). It frees threads and gives the dependency room to recover.

claimcheck.d: Instead of putting a large payload on a queue, store it elsewhere (such as S3) and send only a reference. It keeps messages small and fast, avoids size limits and lets you control retention and access to the data separately.

classimbalance.d: When one class is rare (fraud, churn). Prefer proper metrics, class weights and a tuned decision threshold before resampling; if you oversample (SMOTE), do it only inside training folds. The threshold should be chosen from the cost of each kind of error.

clickjacking.d: Loading your page in an invisible iframe on another site to trick clicks. Prevent with X-Frame-Options: DENY/SAMEORIGIN or CSP frame-ancestors; in the browser test the DENY page did not render in the attacker's frame.

clientcomponent.d: A component marked with 'use client' that ships to the browser and can use state, effects and browser APIs.

closure.d: A function that remembers variables from the scope where it was defined. Closures read the variable at call time, so functions made in a loop all see its final value unless you bind it with a default argument or functools.partial.

cloudevents.d: A CNCF specification for a common event envelope with attributes such as id, source, specversion, type, time and data, so events can move between systems and clouds consistently.

cloudregion.d: A geographic area containing multiple data centers, chosen for latency, price and data-residency requirements.

cloudtrail.d: AWS's audit log of API calls, recording who did what, when and from where.

cloudwatch.d: AWS's monitoring service for metrics, logs and alarms.

cnn.d: A network of stacked convolution, ReLU and pooling layers followed by a classifier, with kernels learned by backpropagation. Early layers find edges, later layers parts and objects. Usually fine-tuned from a pretrained model.

codecoverage.d: A measure of which lines or branches executed during tests. It finds untested areas but says nothing about whether behavior was checked; a test with no assertions still adds coverage. Use it as a flashlight and a floor, not a target.

codesplitting.d: Reducing JavaScript the browser must download, parse and run: split bundles by route and feature with dynamic import(), and tree shake unused exports in ES modules. Analyze the bundle to find heavy dependencies; JavaScript costs more than an equally sized image.

codingassistant.d: Tools from inline completion to agents that read a repository, edit files, run commands and tests, and open pull requests. The engineer still owns the result: supply context, keep tasks small, verify with tests and review, and limit permissions.

cohenkappa.d: A statistic for agreement between two raters (for example a judge model and a human) that corrects raw agreement for chance. A judge that says 'good' almost always can show high raw agreement and a kappa near zero.

coldstart.d: The extra delay when a serverless platform has to start a new instance to handle a request.

coldstartrec.d: A recommender has no interaction history for a new user or item, so collaborative signals are missing. Typical answers are popularity within a segment, content-based features, onboarding questions, and deliberate exploration so new items get exposure.

collabfiltering.d: Recommending items from patterns in many users' behavior rather than item content: people who interacted with similar items will like similar things. Neighborhood methods compare users or items directly; matrix factorization learns latent factors instead.

commandinjection.d: User text reaching a shell command, so ';', '&&', '|' or '$(...)' runs extra commands. Fix: avoid the shell, pass an argument list, validate against an allow-list and run with least privilege.

commitmentcoverage.d: Coverage is the share of eligible usage covered by commitments; utilization is the share of the commitment you actually used. A commitment with discount d only beats on-demand above 1 minus d utilization.

commonjs.d: Node's original module system: require() and module.exports, with __dirname. Selected by .cjs files or by default for .js. Node 22.12 and newer can require() ES modules that have no top-level await.

completiononly.d: Computing the training loss only on the response tokens rather than the prompt, so the model learns to answer instead of reproducing user text. Trainers such as TRL's SFTTrainer offer options for this; check the setting for your dataset format and version.

composite.d: An index on several columns; column order decides which queries it can serve.

composition.d: Building behaviour by giving an object collaborators it uses ("has a" notifier) instead of subclassing ("is a" notifier). It keeps coupling low and makes swapping parts in tests easy; keep inheritance shallow.

concurrency.d: Concurrency is managing many overlapping tasks (often I/O waits); parallelism is running tasks at the same instant on several cores.

configmgmt.d: Describing a machine's desired state in versioned code and having a tool converge it repeatedly, instead of hand-editing servers. Ansible, Puppet, Chef and Salt are examples.

confint.d: A range of plausible values for a true quantity, from a procedure that captures it a stated share of the time (95%) over repeated samples. Narrower with more or less noisy data; always reported alongside the estimate.

confuseddeputy.d: A security flaw where a privileged service is tricked into using its own authority on behalf of a less-privileged party, for example an MCP server calling downstream APIs with broad credentials for the wrong user. Check the caller's authorisation on every call and accept only tokens issued for your service.

connpool.d: A reusable set of open database connections shared by requests, so each request avoids the cost of connecting.

consistenthashing.d: Placing both keys and nodes on a hash ring so that adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys instead of reshuffling everything. Used by Dynamo-style stores, Cassandra, memcached clients and CDNs, usually with virtual nodes for even spread.

constraineddecoding.d: At each generation step, tokens that would break a grammar or JSON Schema are masked out, so the output can only be valid. It guarantees syntax and types, not factual correctness, and underlies provider structured-output features and engines such as Outlines, XGrammar and llama.cpp grammars.

constraint.d: A rule the database enforces on data, such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK or FOREIGN KEY.

consumergroup.d: Consumers sharing a group id divide a topic's partitions among them, each partition to exactly one member, so parallelism is capped by the partition count. Different groups each receive every record independently. Membership changes trigger a rebalance.

consumerlag.d: The gap between the newest offset in a partition and the group's committed offset. It is the main health signal: steady growth means consumers cannot keep up, so optimize processing, add consumers up to the partition count, or add partitions.

container.d: An isolated process that shares the host kernel, with a restricted view of the system (namespaces) and limited resources (cgroups). Lighter and faster to start than a virtual machine.

containerapps.d: Azure's serverless container platform built on Kubernetes, with ingress, revisions and scale to zero.

contbatching.d: Admitting new requests into the running batch and releasing finished ones between every decode step, rather than waiting for a whole static batch to finish. It keeps the GPU full and is standard in modern LLM engines.

contenttype.d: Content-Type says what format the body you are sending or receiving is (application/json, text/html); Accept says which formats the client can read. Many frameworks parse a JSON body only if Content-Type says so.

contexteng.d: Deciding everything a model sees on each call: instructions, tools, retrieved documents, memory and history, within a token budget.

contextmanager.d: An object used in a with block: __enter__ runs on entry and __exit__ always runs on exit, even after an exception. It guarantees cleanup for files, locks and transactions; @contextmanager builds one from a generator.

contextswitch.d: The CPU moving from one thread to another: saving registers, swapping memory mappings and losing warm caches. Costs microseconds directly, more indirectly. The scheduler preempts threads on time slices, so thousands of busy threads waste time switching.

contextualretrieval.d: Prepending a short, document-aware description (title, section path or a model-written one-sentence summary) to each chunk before embedding and keyword indexing, so a chunk like 'the limit is 60 per minute' also says which product it belongs to. Described by Anthropic as reducing failed retrievals.

contextwindow.d: The maximum number of tokens a model can consider at once, covering the prompt, documents, history and its answer.

continuoustraining.d: A pipeline that retrains a model automatically on a schedule, on new data or on a drift alert, and ends in a gated challenger rather than a direct production swap.

contracttest.d: A test that checks a consumer and a provider agree on an interface, without deploying both. In consumer-driven contract testing (Pact), the consumer's expectations are recorded and verified against the provider, replacing many slow end-to-end tests.

controltower.d: A managed AWS service that sets up a landing zone with organization structure, logging, controls and an account factory. Landing zone version 4.0 makes the Security OU and the service integrations optional.

convcommits.d: A commit message format (feat:, fix:, chore:, ! for breaking) that tools read to generate changelogs and decide the next semantic version.

convolution.d: Slide a small kernel over an image, multiply with the patch under it and sum. Each position gives one value, so the output is a feature map showing where that pattern occurs. In a CNN the kernel values are learned.

copyonwrite.d: From pandas 3.0, objects derived from a DataFrame behave as independent copies, so df[mask]['col'] = x no longer changes df (it warns). Use df.loc[mask, 'col'] = x or assign.

corewebvitals.d: Google's field-measured metrics at the 75th percentile: LCP (loading) 2.5 s or less, INP (responsiveness) 200 ms or less, CLS (visual stability) 0.1 or less. INP replaced FID in March 2024.

coroutine.d: The paused function object returned by calling an async def function. Nothing in its body runs until it is awaited or wrapped in a Task.

correlation.d: A number from -1 to 1 for how strongly two numeric columns move together in a straight line. It does not show causation, misses non-linear patterns, and a suspiciously high value with the target often signals leakage.

cors.d: A browser rule that blocks cross-site requests unless the server lists the calling origin in its response headers.

cosine.d: A measure of how different two vectors' directions are, and the usual metric for text embeddings. In pgvector it is the <=> operator.

cosmosdb.d: Azure's globally distributed NoSQL database, where a good partition key and request-unit budget matter.

costallocationtags.d: Resource tags or labels (team, service, environment, cost center) that let billing data be attributed to owners. They must be enforced at creation and activated for cost reporting, and the untagged share is a key health metric.

costanomaly.d: Automatic detection of unusual daily or hourly spend, by provider tools or a simple robust rule such as deviation from a rolling median. It finds a runaway workload within a day instead of at month end.

cot.d: Prompting a model to reason step by step before giving a final answer, which improves multi-step problem solving.

covariateshift.d: A change in the distribution of model inputs while the relationship between inputs and outcome stays the same, such as a new customer segment arriving. It can often be detected without labels but does not always hurt accuracy.

credstuffing.d: Automated login attempts using username and password pairs leaked from other sites, relying on password reuse. Countered by rate limits, breached-password checks, MFA and bot defenses.

criticalrenderpath.d: How the browser turns bytes into pixels: parse HTML into the DOM, CSS into the CSSOM, build the render tree, lay out, paint, composite. CSS and synchronous scripts block it, so use defer or async, inline critical CSS and load the rest without blocking.

cronjob.d: A task scheduled to run at times described by a cron expression such as 0 3 * * * (daily at 03:00).

crossencoder.d: A model that reads the query and a candidate document together and outputs a relevance score. It is more accurate than comparing separate embeddings (a bi-encoder) but too slow for a whole corpus, so it reranks the top 50 to 100 candidates from a first-stage search.

crossval.d: Splitting training data into folds and rotating which fold validates, for a more reliable estimate of performance.

csharp.d: A statically typed, garbage-collected language for the .NET platform: web back ends, cloud services, desktop and mobile apps, and Unity games. Compiles to intermediate language that the runtime JIT-compiles.

csp.d: A response header listing which sources a page may load scripts, styles and frames from. A strict policy limits the damage of XSS even when escaping fails.

cspnonce.d: A fresh random value per response, sent in the Content-Security-Policy header and in each allowed script tag, so injected inline scripts without it are blocked. Roll out with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first.

csproj.d: A short XML file naming the SDK, output type and target framework (net10.0), with switches such as Nullable and ImplicitUsings. A solution groups several projects, for example API, library and tests.

csrecord.d: A concise immutable data type: record Order(int Id, string Customer, decimal UnitPrice) gives a constructor, properties, value-based equality, ToString and 'with' copies. The default for DTOs and domain values.

csrf.d: An attack where a malicious site makes the victim's browser send a state-changing request that carries their cookies. Mitigated by SameSite cookies, Origin checks and CSRF tokens.

csrftoken.d: A random per-session value placed in forms or headers that a forged cross-site request cannot read or guess. Combine with SameSite cookies and Origin checks; compare with a constant-time function.

cssgrid.d: CSS layout mode for two-dimensional rows and columns, for example repeat(auto-fit, minmax(16rem, 1fr)) for responsive card galleries.

cssspecificity.d: The rule that decides which CSS declaration wins: importance, then inline over ID over class, attribute and pseudo-class over element, then later source order. Keep selectors flat to avoid specificity fights.

csv.d: Flat table as text: one row per line, columns separated by commas, fields with commas or newlines in quotes. It has no types (everything is a string), so use a CSV parser, never split(',').

cte.d: A named subquery defined with WITH. It makes long queries readable and allows recursion.

ctrhealth.d: A command Docker runs periodically to tell whether the app inside a container is actually serving, not merely that the process exists. Used by Compose and some platforms for ordering and restarts.

curl.d: The standard command-line HTTP client. Common flags: -i show response headers, -s silent, -X method, -H header, -d body, -v full conversation. 'Copy as cURL' in browser DevTools reproduces a request.

cursorpagination.d: Paging by remembering the last seen key instead of an offset; stays fast on deep pages because it seeks in an index.

dal.d: A single server-only module through which all code reads data and checks authorization, so rules are not scattered.

dataaugmentation.d: Training on randomly altered copies of the examples (shifts, flips, crops, noise) so the model meets the variation it will see in production. Cheap and effective; use only changes that reality also produces.

dataclass.d: A decorator that generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from annotated fields. Options such as frozen=True (immutable, hashable), slots=True and field(default_factory=list) make it the default for plain data-holding classes.

datadrift.d: When live input data or the input-to-outcome relationship changes from what the model was trained on, degrading predictions.

dataframe.d: pandas' labelled table: named columns that may each have a different dtype plus a row index. A Series is one column. The verbs are filter, assign, groupby, merge and clean.

datalake.d: Raw and processed data stored as files (often Parquet) in cheap object storage such as S3. Flexible and inexpensive, but plain files lack transactions and schema enforcement, which is the gap lakehouse table formats fill.

dataloader.d: A batching pattern for GraphQL resolvers that collects keys requested in the same tick and loads them in one query, avoiding one query per item. Create loaders per request so cached data cannot leak between users.

datapoisoning.d: Tampering with training, fine-tuning or embedding data so a model or retrieval index behaves badly or contains hidden triggers. Defend with data provenance, validation and access control on corpora.

datavalidation.d: Automated checks on datasets for schema, ranges, null rates, allowed categories and freshness, run in CI and at every pipeline run. Tools include Great Expectations, pandera and Pydantic models.

dbt.d: A SQL-first transformation tool: write SELECT models, and dbt builds the tables, orders them by dependency, runs tests (unique, not null, accepted values), and generates docs and lineage. Incremental models process only new or changed data.

ddl.d: DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP) defines tables, indexes and views. DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) changes rows. SELECT queries read them.

deadlock.d: Two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds. The database aborts one of them.

debugging.d: Finding why code misbehaves: reproduce with a minimal input, inspect real values with logging or a debugger breakpoint, bisect to narrow the cause, change one thing at a time, and add a regression test. Guessing is the slow path.

decorator.d: A function that takes a function and returns an improved one; @deco above def f means f = deco(f). Always use functools.wraps so the wrapped function keeps its name and signature.

decoratorpattern.d: Wrapping an object with the same interface to add behavior (retries, caching, logging, metrics) without changing it, so wrappers compose: Retry(Cache(Client)). Python's @decorator syntax is the function-level version.

defaultazurecredential.d: An Azure SDK credential that tries managed identity, environment variables and your Azure CLI login in order, so the same code runs locally and in Azure.

delayedlabels.d: The gap between making a prediction and learning the true outcome, such as 30 days for churn. Quality metrics must use matured cohorts whose outcome window has fully passed, or recent rows look better than they are.

deno.d: A secure JavaScript and TypeScript runtime that powers Supabase Edge Functions.

denormalization.d: Deliberately duplicating or precomputing data to speed up reads, at the cost of keeping copies in sync.

depconfusion.d: Attacks where a malicious public package takes the place of an intended one: either by reusing an internal package name at a higher version, or by using a near-identical misspelled name. Scope internal packages and pin their registry.

dependencyinjection.d: Passing a component's collaborators in (constructor or function arguments) instead of having it create or import them. It is the most useful testability pattern: tests pass a small fake. A framework is optional; plain constructor arguments usually suffice.

devcontainer.d: A containerized development environment defined in the repository (devcontainer.json) so every developer, CI job and agent gets the same toolchain. It is also a safer place to let an agent run commands than your own machine.

differentialprivacy.d: A mathematical privacy guarantee: add calibrated noise so that including or excluding any one person's data changes the output only slightly, quantified by a privacy budget epsilon. Used in training (DP-SGD) and statistics release, with an accuracy trade-off.

dijkstra.d: Shortest paths from a source in a graph with non-negative edge weights, using a min-heap to always expand the closest unvisited node, in O((V + E) log V). Bellman-Ford handles negative weights; A-star adds a heuristic to search toward a goal.

discunion.d: A union whose variants share a literal tag field (kind: 'ok' | 'error'). Switching on the tag narrows each case, and a never check enforces exhaustive handling.

distlock.d: Mutual exclusion across processes, in Redis via SET key token NX PX with release by token check in a Lua script. A TTL lock cannot guarantee safety after a long pause or failover; use fencing tokens or database constraints when double execution would cause harm.

dlq.d: A separate queue or topic where messages that repeatedly fail processing (poison messages) are parked with error context, so one bad record does not block the stream. Alert on its growth and build a way to inspect and replay it.

dns.d: The internet's address book: resolves names to IP addresses using records (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT) that resolvers cache for their TTL.

dnsrecord.d: DNS maps names to data via records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), TXT (verification, SPF), NS (delegation), CAA and HTTPS. Each has a TTL telling caches how long to keep it, so lower it before a migration. NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist.

dockercompose.d: A tool and file format for defining and running multi-container apps locally, with networks, volumes and health-gated startup. docker compose up starts the whole stack.

dockerfile.d: A text file of build instructions (base image, copy files, run commands, start command) that produces an image. Instruction order controls layer caching.

dockerimage.d: An immutable, layered package of files and metadata used to start containers. Each Dockerfile instruction can create a layer, and unchanged layers are cached and shared.

domainclassifier.d: Detects multivariate drift by training a classifier to tell reference rows from current rows. An AUC near 0.5 means they are indistinguishable, and the feature importances point to what changed; it catches joint shifts that per-feature tests miss.

domtree.d: The browser's in-memory tree of objects built from the HTML. JavaScript reads and changes it (querySelector, textContent, addEventListener) and CSS styles its nodes.

dotenv.d: A file of KEY=value lines loaded into environment variables by a tool or library. All values are strings and the file usually holds secrets: keep it out of version control and commit a .env.example instead.

dotnet.d: Microsoft's cross-platform runtime and its main language: strong static typing, async/await (which C# pioneered), LINQ, ASP.NET Core and Entity Framework Core, with JIT or Native AOT compilation. Yearly releases, long-term support on even years.

dotnetsdk.d: The SDK has the compiler, build tools and the dotnet command; the runtime only runs compiled apps. Servers need the runtime (or a self-contained publish); developers need the SDK. dotnet --list-sdks shows what is installed.

dotproduct.d: The sum of element-wise products of two vectors; larger means more similar. For unit-length vectors it equals cosine similarity, which is why many systems normalize embeddings and use the cheaper dot product. pgvector exposes the negative inner product as the <#> operator.

dpo.d: A training method that uses pairs of a preferred and a rejected response to nudge a model toward the preferred style, without training a separate reward model or running reinforcement learning as in RLHF. It is applied after SFT, and a beta setting limits how far the model drifts from its starting point.

drift.d: When real infrastructure no longer matches what the code and state describe, usually from manual changes. Detect with scheduled plans.

dropout.d: A regularizer that randomly zeroes activations during training so the network cannot rely on single units, reducing overfitting. It is disabled at evaluation, which is why model.eval() matters.

dtype.d: The single number type shared by every element of an array or column. Fixed-size types wrap around silently (int8: 100 + 100 = -56), an integer column with a missing value becomes float, and float comparison needs isclose.

duckdb.d: An in-process analytical SQL database that runs inside your Python or CLI process, reading Parquet, CSV, JSON and Iceberg directly. It handles many analytics tasks on one machine, up to hundreds of GB, with no cluster to operate.

ducktyping.d: Python cares about what an object can do, not its declared class: anything with a send() method can be used as a notifier. Protocols make that expectation explicit for type checkers.

dunder.d: Special methods with double underscores (__add__, __len__, __iter__, __enter__) that let your objects work with operators, len(), for loops and with blocks. Defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes an object unhashable.

duplicaterows.d: Accidentally repeated records. They over-weight some entities and, when copies land in both training and test sets, make the test score meaningless. Check duplicated() and key uniqueness.

durableworkflow.d: A system (Temporal, AWS Step Functions, Azure Durable Functions, Inngest) that runs multi-step, long-lived processes with persisted state, automatic retries, timers and human-approval waits, resuming after crashes. Use it when a job is really a business process, not one function.

dvc.d: A tool that keeps small pointer files in Git and stores large datasets and models in object storage, so each commit maps to an exact data version. It also offers pipelines and experiment tracking.

dynamodb.d: AWS's serverless key-value and document database, designed around partition keys and known access patterns.

dynprog.d: Solving a problem by combining stored answers to overlapping subproblems, using a table or cache, to avoid exponential recomputation.

dyntyping.d: Python is dynamically typed (names can refer to any type, checked at run time) but strongly typed (it will not silently coerce "3" + 4). Optional type hints let tools check types before running.

ec2.d: AWS's virtual machines, giving full control of the operating system at the cost of managing it.

ecs.d: AWS's container orchestrator. Tasks run on Fargate or EC2, and services keep a desired number running.

eda.d: A short structured investigation before modeling: shape, types, missing values, duplicates, ranges, category labels, target balance, plots and a baseline. It finds defects and leaks while they are cheap to fix.

edgefunction.d: Server-side TypeScript running on Deno near your users, used for webhooks, secrets and third-party calls.

efcore.d: The standard .NET ORM: classes and a DbContext, LINQ queries translated to parameterised SQL, migrations for schema changes. DbContext is scoped and not thread-safe; watch N+1 queries and use projections.

effectivecost.d: Cost after spreading upfront commitment purchases over their term and applying discounts and credits. It makes months comparable and allocation fair, unlike the billed cost on the invoice.

efsearch.d: HNSW tuning knobs: ef_construction is the candidate list size while building the graph (higher gives a better graph and a slower build), and ef_search is the list size at query time (higher improves recall and costs latency). pgvector's defaults are 64 and 40; raise ef_search first when recall is low.

elasticsearch.d: A distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene, queried with JSON Query DSL. OpenSearch is the Apache-2.0 fork started by AWS in 2021. Elasticsearch has been offered under AGPLv3, SSPL and the Elastic License; APIs between the two have diverged.

elicitation.d: An MCP feature letting a server ask the user for missing input during a call, through a form or a URL for out-of-band steps such as signing in. In the 2026-07-28 revision it travels as an input-required result and a retry rather than a server-initiated request.

embedding.d: A list of numbers representing the meaning of text or an image, so similar items sit close together.

embeddingmodel.d: A neural network that maps text, images or code to a fixed-length vector so that similar meaning gives nearby vectors. Choose by testing on your own queries (public leaderboards such as MTEB are a starting point), and record which model and version produced every stored vector.

endianness.d: The byte order of multi-byte values in memory or on the wire: little-endian stores the least significant byte first (x86, most ARM), big-endian the most significant first (network byte order). Binary formats and protocols must specify and convert.

entraid.d: Microsoft's cloud identity service (formerly Azure AD) for users, groups, apps and sign-in.

entratenant.d: Your organization's dedicated Entra ID directory, which holds its users, groups and applications.

envelopeenc.d: Encrypting data with a random data key, then encrypting that key with a master key held in a KMS and storing both together. Rotating the master key only re-wraps data keys.

envvars.d: Configuration values supplied at build or run time, kept out of source code and scoped per environment.

ephemeral.d: A Terraform feature (1.10 and later, write-only arguments from 1.11) that keeps secrets and short-lived values out of the plan and state file.

ephemeralport.d: Listening on port 0 lets the operating system pick a free port, so parallel test files never collide. Read it back with server.address().port and call the server with fetch.

epoll.d: Linux readiness and completion APIs for scalable I/O. epoll lets one thread wait on tens of thousands of sockets and handle only the ready ones (kqueue on BSD and macOS, IOCP on Windows); io_uring batches I/O requests through shared rings. They power event loops in Node, asyncio, Nginx and Redis.

errorboundary.d: A React component that catches render errors in its subtree and shows a fallback instead of unmounting the whole app. Pair it with error reporting such as Sentry.

errorbudget.d: The amount of unreliability an SLO allows (1 minus the SLO), spent on releases and risk. At 99.9% over 30 days it is about 43 minutes of downtime.

errormiddleware.d: An Express middleware with four parameters (err, req, res, next) that runs when a handler throws or rejects.

esm.d: The standard JavaScript module system: import and export, static analysis and top-level await. In Node, .mjs files or "type": "module" select it.

etag.d: An HTTP validator for a resource version. With If-Match on writes it gives optimistic concurrency (412 on conflict); with If-None-Match on reads it enables 304 conditional responses.

etl.d: ETL transforms data before loading it; ELT loads raw data into the warehouse first and transforms it there with SQL. ELT dominates modern stacks because storage and compute are cheap, raw data stays available for reprocessing, and analysts can own the transformations.

ets.d: Forecasts built from exponentially weighted averages of the past with optional trend and seasonal components. A fast, strong baseline for many business series that is often hard to beat with more complex models.

euaiact.d: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, in force since 1 August 2024 with staggered dates: bans on some practices, duties for general-purpose AI model providers, transparency rules for chatbots and synthetic content, and risk-management duties for high-risk systems. High-risk dates were reported delayed to December 2027 and August 2028.

eval.d: Repeatable tests with a dataset and graders that measure whether an AI app got better or worse after a change.

evalcontamination.d: Test cases leaking into prompts, retrieval data or training and fine-tuning data, which inflates scores. Prevent by keeping a held-out set, refreshing cases from new production data and checking that tuning data excludes test inputs.

eventcursor.d: An API endpoint such as GET /events?after=cursor that lets clients read a durable event log at their own pace and recover anything webhooks missed, within a retention window.

eventdelegation.d: Attaching one event listener to a parent and using event.target.closest(...) to find which child was hit: fewer listeners, and it works for elements added later.

eventloop.d: The scheduler in Node.js (and browsers) that runs callbacks when async work finishes, letting one thread serve many requests.

eventualconsistency.d: A model where replicas may briefly disagree but converge if writes stop. It gives low latency and high availability; designs must tolerate stale reads and resolve conflicting writes. Read-your-writes is a common cheap strengthening.

evictionpolicy.d: The maxmemory-policy deciding what Redis does when memory is full: noeviction (reject writes), allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu (evict least used, right for caches), or volatile policies that evict only keys with a TTL.

evidently.d: An open-source Python library that builds drift, data-quality and model-quality reports and test suites from reference and current datasets. The current API uses Report with presets such as DataDriftPreset; the older API (version 0.6.7 and below) differs.

exactlyonce.d: Kafka's guarantee, using the idempotent producer plus transactions and read_committed consumers, that consume-process-produce within Kafka takes effect once. External side effects can still repeat, so it is effectively at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.

exceptions.d: Exceptions signal errors at runtime; try/except (catch in JavaScript) handles them where you can act, such as retry or default. Catch specific errors, never silently swallow them, validate input at the edges, and fail fast with a clear message.

excessiveagency.d: An LLM app risk (OWASP LLM06) where the model has too many tools, too much permission or too little oversight, so a mistake or injection becomes a damaging action. Fix with per-tool least privilege and approval for sensitive steps.

exitstatus.d: A number every command returns when it ends: 0 means success, anything else failure. &&, ||, if and CI pipelines all decide based on it; grep uses 1 for 'no match'.

expandcontract.d: A zero-downtime migration pattern: add the new structure, move data and traffic over, then remove the old one.

expectation.d: Expected value is the probability-weighted average outcome; variance is the average squared distance from it and the standard deviation is its square root. Means without spread and sample size mislead, and skewed data needs medians and percentiles.

explain.d: Runs a query and shows the chosen plan with real timings and row counts.

explainability.d: Making model decisions understandable: interpretable models where stakes are high, and post-hoc methods such as feature importance, SHAP, LIME and counterfactual explanations. Explanations can mislead, so validate them and give people recourse to a human.

expressrouter.d: A mini Express app that groups related routes so they can be mounted under a path such as /v1/users.

externalsecrets.d: A Kubernetes operator that syncs secrets from external stores such as AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault or HashiCorp Vault into Kubernetes Secrets. Git holds only a reference, never the value.

failclosed.d: A design rule: when a security check errors or cannot decide, deny access rather than allow it. Its opposite, failing open, turns outages in a permission service into data exposure.

fairnessmetrics.d: Group measures computed per subgroup: demographic parity (selection rate), equal opportunity (true positive rate), equalized odds (TPR and FPR), predictive parity (precision) and calibration. They conflict when base rates differ, so choose by the harm that matters and document why.

faithfulness.d: Whether every claim in an answer is supported by the provided sources.

faketimers.d: Replace setTimeout and friends with a controllable clock so debounce, retry and expiry logic can be tested instantly and deterministically. In node:test: t.mock.timers.enable() then tick(ms); still marked experimental.

fargate.d: Serverless compute for containers: you define CPU and memory per task, and AWS runs it without servers for you to manage.

fastapi.d: An ASGI Python web framework that builds request validation, serialization and OpenAPI docs from type hints and Pydantic models. async def endpoints run on the loop; plain def endpoints run in a thread pool.

fd.d: A small integer the kernel gives a process for an open file, pipe, socket or device (0, 1 and 2 are stdin, stdout, stderr). Each process has a limit (ulimit -n); leaking descriptors eventually causes too many open files errors.

featureeng.d: Turning raw columns into inputs a model can learn from: imputing missing values, transforming skewed numbers, encoding categories, extracting date parts and building aggregates. Every feature must be computable at prediction time without peeking at the future.

featureflag.d: A runtime switch that turns code on or off per user or percentage without redeploying. It separates deploying from releasing and doubles as a kill switch.

featurestore.d: A system that stores and serves consistent features for both training and online prediction.

fetchapi.d: The browser (and Node 18+) API for HTTP requests: fetch(url) returns a promise of a Response. It rejects only on network failure, so check response.ok before calling response.json().

fewshot.d: Including a few input and output examples in the prompt to show the model the format and style you want.

fifoqueue.d: A queue type with ordering guarantees. In SQS FIFO, ordering applies per message group id and deduplication ids suppress repeats within a window, at lower throughput than standard queues. Use a group id like the customer or order id.

filepermissions.d: Unix access control: each file has an owner, group and read/write/execute bits for user, group and other (for example 640 or rw-r-----). chmod and chown change them, umask sets defaults, and sudo runs one command as root. Never fix errors with chmod 777.

filteredsearch.d: Nearest-neighbor search restricted by metadata such as tenant or date. Post-filtering an ANN result can return fewer than k rows when the filter is selective; remedies include iterative index scans (pgvector 0.8+), partial or partitioned indexes, and engines with filter-aware graph traversal.

finalhandler.d: What runs when the middleware stack is exhausted: a 404 if nothing answered, a 500 if an error was unhandled. Express shows the stack trace only when NODE_ENV is not production.

finetuning.d: Further training of a model on a smaller dataset to specialize its behavior, format or domain knowledge.

finops.d: The practice of making cloud cost visible, attributable and optimizable so engineering, finance and product decide together where spend creates value. Its framework loops through Inform, Optimize and Operate.

fk.d: A column that references another table's key so the database can reject orphaned rows.

flakytest.d: A test that passes and fails on the same code, usually from real time, unseeded randomness, shared state, test order, network calls or fixed UI sleeps. Flakiness trains teams to ignore red builds; quarantine it, find the cause, then fix or delete.

flashattention.d: A fused GPU attention kernel that computes attention in tiles without writing the full attention matrix to slow memory. It makes long contexts faster and far cheaper in memory, and is on by default in good engines.

flexbox.d: CSS layout mode for arranging items along one axis, with gap, justify-content, align-items and flex-grow; ideal for toolbars, navigation and centring.

flexconsumption.d: The recommended serverless hosting plan for Azure Functions, replacing the Linux Consumption plan retiring in September 2028.

fluidcompute.d: Vercel's execution model that reuses function instances for concurrent requests and bills mainly for active CPU time.

fluxks.d: The Flux resource that applies a path from a source (Git, OCI or a bucket) to the cluster on an interval, with prune, health checks, dependsOn ordering and optional SOPS decryption.

a: FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification
focus.d: An open, vendor-neutral schema for billing data from clouds and SaaS, so exports from different providers can be queried the same way. Core columns include BilledCost, EffectiveCost, ChargeCategory, ServiceName, SubAccountId and Tags.

forcewithlease.d: git push --force-with-lease overwrites a remote branch only if it still points where you last saw it, so you cannot destroy a teammate's newer commits. Prefer it to plain --force after rebasing your own branch.

foreach.d: Two ways to create many resources. count addresses them by position, so removing one shifts the others and forces destroy and recreate; for_each addresses them by stable keys, so adding or removing an item affects only that item.

forupdate.d: Reads rows and locks them so no one else can modify them until your transaction ends.

frontdoor.d: Azure's global entry point combining CDN, routing and WAF.

fstring.d: A string literal prefixed with f that evaluates expressions inside braces, with format specs such as {x:.2f} or {n:,}. {x!r} shows the repr and {x=} prints the expression and its value; it is the standard way to build text in Python.

gbdt.d: An ensemble built sequentially: each small decision tree is fitted to the errors of the model so far and added with a learning rate. It is the default strong model for tabular data. Early stopping on a validation set picks the number of trees; a random forest instead averages independent deep trees.

gcvsmanual.d: How a language frees memory: garbage collection (Go, Java, C#, Python, JavaScript) finds unused objects at runtime, trading overhead and pauses for safety; ownership (Rust) proves it at compile time; manual management (C, C++) gives control and memory-safety bugs.

generator.d: A function with yield (or a generator expression) that produces values lazily, pausing at each yield and resuming on the next request. It keeps memory flat for large or infinite streams.

getclaims.d: Supabase method that verifies the access token and returns its claims, locally when the project uses asymmetric signing keys. Preferred for server-side checks.

getuser.d: Supabase method that asks the Auth server for the current user on every call, so it reflects revocations and fresh data.

gguf.d: A single-file model format used by llama.cpp (and wrappers like Ollama and LM Studio) with quantization types such as Q4_K_M and Q8_0, designed to run on CPUs, Apple Silicon and GPUs with layers offloaded as memory allows.

ghactions.d: GitHub's built-in automation: YAML workflows triggered by events that run jobs on hosted or self-hosted runners. Harden it with read-only tokens, SHA-pinned actions and OIDC.

gil.d: CPython's global interpreter lock: in the default build only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time. A free-threaded build, experimental in 3.13 and supported but optional from 3.14, removes it.

gin.d: An inverted index for values that hold many elements, such as jsonb, arrays and full-text search.

gitbranch.d: A movable label pointing at a commit. Creating one is instant and committing moves the label forward; git switch -c name creates and switches.

gitignore.d: Lists patterns of files Git should not track (build output, dependencies, secrets). It affects only untracked files; files already committed need git rm --cached, and history keeps them.

gitobjects.d: Git stores content-addressed objects: blobs (file contents), trees (directories), commits (a tree, parents, author, message) and tags. A commit id hashes everything behind it, so history is tamper-evident and immutable; branches and tags are just refs pointing at commits.

gitops.d: Operating infrastructure and Kubernetes by making Git the single source of truth; a controller continuously reconciles the live system to what is in Git.

gitremote.d: A named copy of the repository elsewhere, usually origin on GitHub or GitLab. clone, fetch, pull and push exchange commits with it.

gitstash.d: Shelves uncommitted changes on a stack so you can switch tasks with a clean working tree; git stash pop restores them.

gitworktree.d: A second (or third) working directory attached to the same repository, each on its own branch. Handy for running several tasks or coding agents in parallel without file conflicts, then reviewing and merging each through a normal pull request.

globbing.d: The shell expands patterns such as *.txt, ? and [ab] into matching file names before the program starts, so the program never sees the star. Quote the pattern to pass it through literally.

goldenset.d: A fixed, curated set of labeled examples, including hard cases and important slices, used to compare every candidate the same way. Refresh it on a schedule and keep a separate untouched holdout, or repeated tuning leaks into it.

goldensignals.d: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation: the four metrics Google SRE recommends monitoring for any user-facing service.

goroutine.d: Go's lightweight concurrency: goroutines are cheap functions scheduled by the runtime onto a few OS threads (millions are feasible); channels pass values between them; context.Context carries cancellation and deadlines. Use the race detector (go test -race).

gqa.d: An attention variant where many query heads share a smaller number of key and value heads. It shrinks the KV cache several-fold with little quality loss, raising the number of concurrent sequences a GPU can serve.

gracefulshutdown.d: Stopping a server by refusing new requests, finishing in-flight ones and closing connections before exiting.

gradcheck.d: Verifies a hand-written backward pass by nudging each weight up and down, measuring the loss change and comparing with the backprop gradient. Relative differences around 1e-7 pass; around 1e-3 mean a bug.

gradientcalc.d: A derivative is the rate of change of a function; the gradient is the vector of partial derivatives pointing toward steepest increase. Gradient descent steps against it, and the chain rule is what backpropagation applies layer by layer.

gradientdescent.d: Training by repeatedly moving each parameter a small step opposite its gradient of the loss. Backpropagation computes those gradients efficiently. Variants (SGD with momentum, Adam) differ in how they scale and smooth the steps.

gradualtyping.d: A typing approach where annotated and unannotated code mix freely: unannotated values are Any and are not checked, so you can add types module by module.

graphql.d: A query language and runtime where the client specifies exactly which fields it needs from a typed schema. It cuts over-fetching but complicates caching, cost control and N+1 resolver queries.

graphqlcost.d: Defenses that cap query depth, computed cost, pagination size and execution time, since a single query can fan out into thousands of resolver calls. Rate limit by cost, not by request count.

graphqlfederation.d: An architecture where several teams own subgraphs that a gateway composes into one supergraph. It scales ownership across teams and adds a gateway to operate.

graphtraversal.d: Visiting nodes of a graph. BFS uses a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS goes deep and suits cycle detection and topological sort.

greedymatch.d: Quantifiers like + and * match as much as possible (greedy), so <.+> spans from the first < to the last >. Add ? (<.+?>) or use a negated class ([^>]+) to stop at the first delimiter.

groundedcitation.d: Having the answer cite the retrieved chunk or document it relies on (by id or index) and checking in code that each citation refers to a chunk that was actually retrieved and supports the claim. Makes answers auditable and exposes unsupported statements.

groupby.d: Collapses rows with equal values into groups so aggregates like COUNT and SUM run per group.

grpc.d: A remote-procedure-call framework using Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2: compact, strongly typed and streaming-capable. Common between internal services; browsers need a proxy layer.

grpcdeadline.d: An absolute time limit set on a call that propagates to downstream calls so slow chains stop instead of piling up work. Every gRPC call should set one.

grpcstreaming.d: gRPC's four call types: unary, server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional streaming, all multiplexed over HTTP/2. Useful for feeds, uploads and chat-like flows.

grpcweb.d: Ways to call gRPC services from browsers, which cannot speak native gRPC: gRPC-Web through a proxy, or the Connect protocol, which supports plain HTTP and JSON as well as gRPC.

guardrails.d: Classifiers or rules that screen model inputs and outputs for attacks, unsafe content or policy violations. Useful for noise reduction, but they are bypassable and not a substitute for permission checks in code.

hallucination.d: Fluent model output that is false or unsupported, because the model predicts plausible text rather than retrieving facts.

hashmap.d: A structure giving average O(1) lookup, insert and delete by key through a hash function. Backs dictionaries, sets, caches and counters.

havingclause.d: Filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation (for example HAVING SUM(total) > 100); WHERE filters rows before grouping.

hcl.d: The configuration language of Terraform and OpenTofu, with blocks, expressions, loops (for_each) and functions, designed to be readable by humans.

a: Cannot set headers after they are sent
headerssent.d: Node error when code tries to set status or headers after the response has started, usually because two code paths both responded (a handler sent a response and also called next, or a missing return). Use 'return res.json(...)'.

headref.d: The pointer to where you are now, usually a branch that points to a commit. Detached HEAD means it points straight at a commit, so new commits belong to no branch.

heapq.d: A heap-backed structure that returns the smallest (or largest) item first in O(log n); used by schedulers, top-K and Dijkstra.

helm.d: The Kubernetes package manager: charts bundle templated manifests with per-environment values and are installed as versioned releases that can be upgraded and rolled back. Kustomize is the template-free alternative using overlays and patches.

helmet.d: An Express middleware that sets protective HTTP headers such as Content-Security-Policy and X-Content-Type-Options.

hexagonal.d: Also called ports and adapters: the core domain defines ports (interfaces it needs) and adapters (Postgres, Stripe, HTTP) plug into them, so dependencies point inward. The core is testable in milliseconds and survives framework or vendor swaps.

histogram.d: A bar chart of how many values fall into each range. It shows shape, skew, gaps and outliers; one extreme value can compress all the real data into a single bar, which is itself a diagnosis.

hmac.d: A keyed hash that proves a message came from someone holding the shared secret and was not altered. Used to sign webhooks; verify it with a constant-time comparison.

hnsw.d: Hierarchical Navigable Small World: a graph-based approximate nearest-neighbour index with fast search and high recall.

hpa.d: A Kubernetes controller that changes the number of Pod replicas based on metrics such as CPU utilization. It needs resource requests to compute utilization.

hpsearch.d: Choosing model settings by trying candidates against validation data. Random search usually beats grid search for the same budget; Optuna adds adaptive search and pruning. Each search makes the validation score optimistic, so keep a final holdout or use nested cross-validation.

hsts.d: The Strict-Transport-Security header tells browsers to use HTTPS only for a host for a stated period, preventing downgrade and cookie-stripping attacks. Enable it after confirming HTTPS works everywhere; preload lists make it apply from the first visit.

http.d: The request and response protocol of the web: methods, status codes and headers. HTTP/2 multiplexes requests; HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP.

http3.d: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, a UDP-based transport with built-in TLS 1.3. Streams are independent, so a lost packet delays only its own stream (HTTP/2 over TCP suffers head-of-line blocking), setup is faster, and connections survive network switches. Advertised via Alt-Svc or an HTTPS DNS record.

httpheaders.d: Name: value lines that carry metadata: the body's format (Content-Type), formats the client accepts (Accept), credentials (Authorization), the new resource's address (Location), caching rules (Cache-Control).

httpmethod.d: The verb of a request. GET reads and is safe; POST creates or triggers an action; PUT replaces; PATCH changes part; DELETE removes. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST is not by default.
