httponlycookie.d: A cookie JavaScript cannot read, so XSS cannot steal it. Injected code can still act as the user, so HttpOnly limits damage rather than preventing XSS. Pair with Secure (HTTPS only) and SameSite.

httpstatus.d: A three-digit result in every response: 2xx success (201 Created, 204 No Content), 3xx redirect, 4xx the client's fault (400, 401, 403, 404, 422, 429), 5xx the server's fault (500, 502, 503).

hubspoke.d: A network layout where workload networks (spokes) attach to a central hub, such as an AWS Transit Gateway or an Azure Virtual WAN or hub VNet, that centralizes egress, inspection and on-premises links. It needs non-overlapping address ranges.

humanapproval.d: Requiring a person to approve an irreversible or outward action (send, pay, delete, deploy) before an agent performs it. The approval screen must show the real arguments.

hybridsearch.d: Combining vector search with keyword search and merging the results to catch both meaning and exact terms.

hyde.d: A query-rewriting trick: have a model write a hypothetical answer, embed that instead of (or alongside) the short question, and search with it. It can help when questions and documents are phrased very differently, but costs an extra model call and can drift.

hydration.d: Attaching event handlers and state to server-rendered HTML in the browser so it becomes interactive.

iaas.d: Renting virtual machines, storage and networks and managing everything above them yourself.

iac.d: Managing servers, networks and cloud services through versioned text files instead of manual console clicks, so environments are reviewable and repeatable.

iacscan.d: Automated checks on infrastructure code before apply: tflint and validate for correctness, Trivy or Checkov for insecure configuration (open security groups, unencrypted storage), and terraform test or tofu test for assertions about plans and applies.

iam.d: AWS's service for controlling who can do what: users, roles and policies that allow or deny actions on resources.

iamrole.d: An AWS identity with no permanent credentials; a principal assumes it and receives temporary credentials.

icebergtable.d: An open table format (like Delta Lake and Apache Hudi) that adds ACID commits, schema evolution, time travel and row-level updates and deletes to Parquet files in object storage. A catalog (often a REST catalog) tracks tables, so several engines can share them: the lakehouse model.

idempotencykey.d: A client-generated unique key sent with an unsafe request (usually POST). The server stores the result and replays it on a retry, so a repeated request cannot repeat its side effect.

idempotent.d: An operation that has the same effect whether it runs once or many times, which makes retries safe.

identity.d: An auto-incrementing integer column, the modern replacement for serial in Postgres.

identitycenter.d: The AWS workforce single sign-on service: people sign in with the company identity provider and receive short-lived role sessions in each account through permission sets, with no long-lived human keys.

idor.d: A bug where changing an identifier in a request (an invoice id, a user id) returns or modifies another user's record because the server never checks ownership. The most common form of Broken Access Control.

ieee754.d: The standard binary format for decimals: a sign, exponent and fraction (a double has 53 bits of precision). Many decimals such as 0.1 are inexact, NaN is not equal to itself, and sums accumulate error, so compare with tolerance and never use floats for money.

igw.d: The VPC component that gives public subnets a route to and from the internet.

imagedigest.d: The content hash that uniquely identifies an exact image. Unlike a tag, it never moves, so pinning by digest guarantees reproducible deploys and rollbacks.

imagetensor.d: A greyscale image is a (rows, columns) array of brightness values; colour adds a channel axis of 3 (red, green, blue). Channel order (last or first) and value range (0-255 or 0-1) must match between training and serving.

immutableinfra.d: Replacing servers with freshly built images instead of patching them in place, so running machines never drift. Images are often baked with Packer and rolled out with Terraform or an autoscaling group.

implicitfeedback.d: Behavior that suggests preference without stating it: clicks, views, watch time, purchases. It is plentiful but noisy, and a missing interaction does not mean dislike, so models treat observed events as positives with varying confidence and sample or down-weight the rest.

inboxpattern.d: Recording each incoming event id in a table with a unique key before processing, so a duplicate delivery inserts nothing and is skipped. It is the receiving-side counterpart to the outbox pattern.

incidentresponse.d: The prepared process for handling a security incident: roles, severity levels, runbooks, detection, containment, eradication, recovery and a postmortem. Rehearsal matters more than document length.

index.d: A separate sorted structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table.

indirectinjection.d: Prompt injection delivered through content the model processes, such as a web page, email, ticket, document or tool description, rather than typed by the user. The attacker never talks to the model directly.

innerjoin.d: Returns only rows that have a match in both tables.

inplaceresize.d: Changing a running Pod's CPU and memory requests and limits without restarting it. It reached stable in Kubernetes 1.35 and makes vertical scaling less disruptive; the Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommends the right sizes.

insyncreplicas.d: The set of replicas of a partition that are caught up with its leader. With acks=all, a write is acknowledged once all in-sync replicas have it, and min.insync.replicas sets how many must exist for writes to be accepted, trading availability for durability.

interactiverebase.d: git rebase -i lists commits so you can reorder, squash, fixup, reword, edit or drop them, curating clean history before review. git commit --fixup with git rebase -i --autosquash folds corrections into the right commits automatically.

inventory.d: The list of managed hosts and their groups, as a static YAML or INI file or generated by a plugin that reads a cloud API such as aws_ec2. Group and host variables hang off it.

invertedindex.d: The core search data structure: for every term, the list of documents containing it (with frequencies and positions), like the index at the back of a book. Queries become list lookups and merges, then scoring. Lucene stores it in immutable, compressed segments.

ipam.d: Centrally planning and allocating non-overlapping address ranges per account, region and network, using a tool such as AWS VPC IPAM or a Git-tracked plan. Overlaps block peering and shared hubs.

iqrrule.d: Flags values above Q3 + 1.5 x (Q3 - Q1) or below Q1 - 1.5 x (Q3 - Q1) as outliers. A quick screening rule, not proof of an error; real heavy-tailed data will produce many flags.

isolation.d: How much a transaction can see of others' concurrent changes. Postgres offers Read Committed (default), Repeatable Read and Serializable.

isr.d: Serving a pre-built page and regenerating it in the background after a set time or on demand.

iterator.d: An iterable can produce an iterator (iter(x)); an iterator hands out items with next() and raises StopIteration when finished. Iterators are single-use, which is why a consumed generator appears empty the second time.

itertools.d: A standard library module of building blocks for lazy iteration: islice takes the first n, chain joins iterables, groupby groups consecutive items, and batched (3.12+) yields fixed-size chunks.

ivfflat.d: An approximate vector index that clusters vectors into lists and searches only the nearest ones. It needs data present before it is built.

jit.d: Compiling hot code to machine code at run time, as the JVM, .NET, V8 and PyPy do, combining portability with high steady-state speed at the cost of warm-up. Compilers translate ahead of time; interpreters execute step by step; many languages compile to bytecode first.

join.d: Combines rows from two tables where a condition, usually matching keys, is true.

json.d: Text format for objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true/false and null. Double quotes only, no comments, no trailing commas. The default language of web APIs and structured logs.

jsonmode.d: A provider setting that makes the model emit syntactically valid JSON but enforces no particular schema, so keys and types can still be wrong or missing. Schema-constrained structured outputs are the stronger option where available.

jsonrpc.d: A lightweight remote-procedure protocol using JSON: requests with an id, method and params, responses with a result or error, and id-less notifications. MCP carries all its messages in JSON-RPC over its transports.

jsonschema.d: A standard vocabulary for describing the shape of JSON: types, required properties, enums and nesting. It is shared by OpenAPI, tool definitions and LLM structured outputs, though each provider supports only a subset of its keywords.

jsx.d: A syntax extension that lets you write UI as markup inside JavaScript or TypeScript. A compiler turns it into function calls that produce a description of the UI.

jvm.d: The Java Virtual Machine runs bytecode with a just-in-time compiler, giving strong steady-state performance after warm-up, mature garbage collectors (G1, ZGC) and a huge ecosystem. Java 21 added virtual threads; Kotlin, Scala and Clojure also run on it.

jwks.d: A published set of public keys used to verify JWT signatures without sharing a secret.

jwt.d: A signed token containing claims such as the user id. Servers verify the signature to trust it without a database lookup.

k8sdeployment.d: A Kubernetes object that keeps a set number of identical Pods running and rolls out new versions gradually with rollback support. It manages ReplicaSets underneath.

k8singress.d: Kubernetes resources that route external HTTP(S) traffic to Services, handled by an ingress controller. The newer Gateway API is the successor design with richer routing.

k8spod.d: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: one or more containers sharing a network namespace and storage. Pods are disposable and replaced, not repaired.

k8srbac.d: Kubernetes access control: roles list allowed verbs on resources, bindings attach them to users or ServiceAccounts. Give each workload its own minimal ServiceAccount.

k8sscheduler.d: How Pods are matched to nodes: nodeSelector and affinity attract Pods, taints repel them unless tolerated, topology spread constraints and anti-affinity spread replicas across zones and nodes, and priority classes decide who is preempted when the cluster is full.

k8sservice.d: A stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of Pods chosen by labels. Other workloads call the Service, not individual Pods.

kafka.d: A distributed, replicated, append-only commit log for event streaming. Producers append records to topics, consumers read at their own offsets, and records are retained for a set time so streams can be replayed. Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper in favor of KRaft.

kafkaconnect.d: A framework and connector catalog for moving data in and out of Kafka without custom code: source connectors (such as Debezium for CDC) and sink connectors (S3, warehouses, search indexes). Handles offsets, retries and scaling of the copy tasks.

kafkaoffset.d: A consumer's position in a partition, committed to the internal __consumer_offsets topic. Committing after processing gives at-least-once delivery; committing before gives at-most-once. Resetting offsets replays history.

kafkapartition.d: A topic is a named stream of records, split into partitions: ordered, append-only logs spread over brokers. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, and the record key decides which one. Partitions can be added but never removed.

kestrel.d: ASP.NET Core's built-in cross-platform web server. Usually run behind a reverse proxy or load balancer that terminates TLS; set forwarded-headers handling so the app sees the real client address and scheme.

keyvault.d: An Azure service for storing secrets, keys and certificates with access controlled by RBAC.

kms.d: A managed service that creates and protects encryption keys in hardware and performs encrypt, decrypt and signing operations on request. Access is controlled by IAM policy and every call is logged.

kraft.d: Kafka's built-in Raft-based metadata quorum that replaced ZooKeeper. Kafka 4.0 (18 March 2025) removed ZooKeeper entirely; clusters must migrate to KRaft while on a 3.x release before upgrading, and managed services such as MSK may require a new cluster.

kstest.d: A test that compares two numeric samples by the maximum distance between their empirical cumulative distributions. On large samples its p-value becomes tiny for trivial shifts, so read the statistic as an effect size too.

kustomize.d: A template-free way to customize Kubernetes manifests: a base plus per-environment overlays that patch images, replicas and names. It is built into kubectl and used by both Argo CD and Flux.

kvcache.d: Stored attention data for tokens already processed, so each new token is cheap to generate; the basis of prompt caching.

kwargs.d: Parameters that collect extra positional arguments into a tuple (*args) and extra keyword arguments into a dict (**kwargs). Handy for wrappers and decorators that pass everything through, but they weaken the visible signature if overused.

lagfeatures.d: Model inputs built from the target's own past: the value k steps ago, or rolling means and standard deviations. Every window must end at or before the forecast origin (shift by at least the horizon) or the model sees the future.

lambda.d: AWS's function-as-a-service: runs your code on events, scales per request and bills per millisecond, with a 15-minute maximum run.

landingzone.d: A governed multi-account (or multi-subscription) foundation with organization structure, identity, guardrails, logging, security tooling, networking and account vending, so new workloads start compliant. AWS Control Tower and the Azure landing zone reference architecture are examples.

langfuse.d: An open-source platform for tracing LLM applications, managing prompts and running evaluations with datasets and scores.

lazyeval.d: Computing values only when needed, one at a time, instead of building everything up front. Python 3.15 also adds explicit lazy imports (the lazy keyword) so modules load on first use, reducing startup time.

leakage.d: Information from the test set or the future leaking into training, giving misleadingly good results.

learningrate.d: How far each gradient step moves the weights. Too small trains slowly, too large overshoots and the loss blows up (up to nan). The first hyperparameter to tune, usually by factors of 10.

leastprivilege.d: Granting only the permissions needed for a task and nothing more, to limit the damage of mistakes and breaches.

leftjoin.d: Keeps every row from the left table; columns from the right are NULL when there is no match.

lethaltrifecta.d: The dangerous combination in an AI agent of access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally. With all three, a prompt injection can leak data; remove one leg to break the attack path.

libuv.d: The C library behind Node's event loop and thread pool; it handles async I/O across operating systems.

lightgbm.d: A fast gradient boosting library from Microsoft that grows trees leaf-wise and supports native categorical features. num_leaves is the main complexity control; it can overfit small datasets unless min_child_samples is raised.

linalg.d: A vector is a list of numbers (a point, a feature set, an embedding); a matrix is a grid, and matrix multiplication applies a transformation to many vectors at once. Dot product and norms give cosine similarity; neural network layers are matrix multiplications plus nonlinearities.

linq.d: Language-integrated query: Where, Select, GroupBy, OrderBy and Sum over any sequence, like array methods in JavaScript. Queries are lazy: they run when enumerated, so call ToList() for a snapshot.

linter.d: A linter flags likely bugs and bad practice (ESLint, Ruff, Clippy); a formatter rewrites code to one style (Prettier, Black, gofmt). Together with a type checker they give instant, automatic feedback on human and AI-written code.

listcomp.d: A one-expression way to build a list, dict or set from an iterable with an optional filter: [n * n for n in xs if n % 2 == 0]. Clear for simple transforms; switch to a loop when the logic needs several steps.

llmjudge.d: Using a language model to score another model's output against a rubric; useful at scale but needs calibration against human labels.

llmstreaming.d: Server-sent events deliver the reply piece by piece: message_start, content_block_start, many content_block_delta, content_block_stop, message_delta (stop_reason, cumulative usage), message_stop. Errors can arrive after a 200 status.

llmtoken.d: A chunk of text, often a word piece, that a model reads and writes as an integer id. Models are priced and limited in tokens.

loadbalancer.d: Spreads incoming traffic across healthy instances; L4 forwards TCP connections, L7 routes by HTTP host, path or header and can terminate TLS.

lockfile.d: A file recording the exact version and integrity hash of every resolved dependency, direct and transitive. Install from it with npm ci so builds are reproducible and silent upgrades cannot slip in.

logarchive.d: A dedicated account that receives organization-wide audit logs such as CloudTrail, with write-once retention and tight access, so an attacker in a workload account cannot erase evidence.

logcompaction.d: A cleanup policy that keeps only the latest record per key instead of deleting by age, turning a topic into a changelog of current state. A record with a null value (tombstone) removes a key. Used for state, configuration and CDC topics.

loggedmodel.d: The MLflow 3 entity that represents a model as a first-class object, linking it to its code version, parameters, evaluation runs and traces. It moves model tracking beyond a purely run-centric view.

longtask.d: A main-thread task over 50 ms blocks input and hurts INP. Break work into slices and yield between them (scheduler.yield, setTimeout), debounce high-frequency events, avoid layout thrashing, or move computation into a Web Worker.

lora.d: Low-Rank Adaptation: freeze a pretrained model and train small low-rank matrices added to selected layers. It cuts trainable parameters, memory and storage by orders of magnitude, so one base model can serve many cheap task-specific adapters.

lossfunction.d: The single number that says how wrong the model is, which training minimises. Binary cross-entropy punishes confident wrong probabilities steeply; at a coin-flip prediction it equals ln 2 = 0.693.

lostinthemiddle.d: The observed tendency of language models to use information at the start and end of a long input better than information buried in the middle. A reason to retrieve fewer, better passages and to place critical facts and the question where they are easy to use.

lrucache.d: A decorator that stores results of a function keyed by its arguments, evicting the least recently used when full. Use it only on pure functions of hashable arguments; on methods it keeps self alive.

lsp.d: A standard protocol by which an editor talks to a language server for completion, go-to-definition, rename and diagnostics. It lets VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, Neovim and others share one implementation per language.

luascript.d: A script executed atomically on the Redis server (EVAL, or Functions in newer versions). The right tool for check-and-update logic such as rate limiters, safe lock release and inventory decrements. In a cluster all keys must be in one slot.

managedidentity.d: An identity Azure creates and rotates for a resource, letting apps authenticate without storing secrets.

mapping.d: The schema of a search index. Key choice: text (analyzed, full-text) versus keyword (exact, for filters, sorting, aggregations). Dynamic mapping guesses types and can cause wrong types or a mapping explosion, so define mappings explicitly and reindex to change a type.

mase.d: Forecast error divided by the in-sample error of a naive (often seasonal naive) forecast, so values below 1 mean the model beats the baseline and the metric is comparable across series of different scale. Unlike MAPE it stays defined when actual values are zero.

massassignment.d: Binding a request body straight onto a database entity lets a client set fields it should not (isAdmin, ownerId, price). Bind to dedicated input records and copy allowed fields explicitly.

matrixfactorization.d: Approximating the user-item interaction matrix as the product of a user factor matrix and an item factor matrix with k latent dimensions, so a score is a dot product. ALS and BPR are common training methods for implicit feedback, and the item factors work as embeddings.

matryoshka.d: Embeddings trained so that the first N dimensions already form a useful smaller embedding, letting you truncate (and re-normalize) vectors to save storage and latency with modest quality loss. Some embedding APIs expose this as a dimensions parameter.

mcp.d: An open protocol that lets AI applications discover and use external tools, data and prompts through a standard interface.

mcpclient.d: The component inside a host application that speaks MCP to exactly one server: it discovers tools, resources and prompts, sends calls and returns results to the host. The host decides which calls the model may make.

mcphost.d: The AI application the user runs (a chat assistant, an IDE or an agent framework). It owns the model, the user interface and the security decisions such as confirmation prompts, and contains one MCP client per connected server.

mcpresource.d: Read-only context a server exposes at a URI (a file, a schema, a document) for the host application to load. Application-controlled, unlike tools, which the model chooses to call.

mcpserver.d: A program that exposes tools, resources or prompts over MCP; the client inside an AI app connects to it.

medallion.d: Organizing data into layers: bronze (raw, append-only, as received), silver (cleaned, deduplicated, typed), gold (business-ready marts and metrics). Each layer can be rebuilt from the one below, which makes fixes and backfills safe.

mediaquery.d: A CSS condition such as @media (min-width: 48rem) or (prefers-color-scheme: dark) that applies rules only on matching screens or user settings; the basis of responsive, mobile-first design.

memoryhierarchy.d: Registers, L1, L2 and L3 caches, RAM, SSD, disk and the network trade size for speed: about 1 ns for L1, around 100 ns for RAM, roughly 100 microseconds for SSD, milliseconds for disk and across a network. Software performance is mostly about staying high in the hierarchy.

mergeconflict.d: Happens when two branches change the same lines. Git writes <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers; edit to the final text, git add, then commit (or git merge --abort).

messagequeue.d: A durable buffer between producers and consumers. Producers enqueue work and return; workers dequeue, process and acknowledge. It smooths bursts and isolates failures, at the cost of eventual results and duplicate deliveries.

messagesapi.d: Anthropic's chat endpoint: you POST a model, max_tokens, optional system prompt and a list of user/assistant messages, with x-api-key, anthropic-version and content-type headers. The reply holds content blocks, stop_reason and usage.

methodchaining.d: Writing a data transformation as a chain of calls (df.assign(...).query(...).groupby(...)), each returning a new object. Reads like a recipe, avoids mutating the original, and is easy to debug step by step.

mfa.d: Requiring more than one kind of proof to sign in, such as a password plus a code or passkey. Phishing-resistant factors (passkeys, security keys) are stronger than SMS or TOTP codes.

mgmtgroup.d: A container above subscriptions in Azure that lets you apply Azure Policy and role assignments once and inherit them down a hierarchy such as Platform, Landing Zones, Sandbox and Decommissioned.

microtask.d: Short callbacks, such as promise reactions, that run as soon as the current code finishes and before the event loop continues.

middleware.d: A function that sits between request and response, able to inspect, modify or end the request, or pass it to the next function.

migration.d: A versioned script that changes the database schema so every environment evolves the same way.

minimalapi.d: Endpoints defined in a few lines of Program.cs: app.MapGet('/', () => ...). Parameters bind from route, query, body and DI services by type and name. The low-ceremony default style for new services.

minimalrepro.d: The smallest input and code that still shows a bug, every time. Shrinking it often reveals the cause, and it is the most useful thing to attach to a bug report or a question.

missingvalues.d: Gaps in data, shown as NaN in pandas. NaN is not equal to itself and spreads through arithmetic. Decide deliberately whether to fill (median, a flag), drop or keep, and ask why the value is missing.

mixedprecision.d: Running most math in 16-bit numbers (torch.autocast) for about half the memory and faster matrix operations. bfloat16 has fp32's range and usually needs no loss scaling; float16 needs a GradScaler to avoid underflow.

mlflowrun.d: One execution of training code recorded with its parameters, metrics, tags, code version and artifacts, grouped under a named experiment. Runs let you compare attempts and rebuild any result.

mlops.d: The practices for building, deploying, monitoring and retraining ML models reliably in production.

mlp.d: Layers of neurons where each layer's outputs feed the next, with non-linear activations between them. A hidden layer lets the network bend its decision boundary and solve problems like XOR.

mmr.d: A re-selection method that balances relevance to the query against novelty versus already chosen results, so the top-k are not five near-duplicates of the same passage.

modelalias.d: A movable, human-readable name such as champion or challenger that points at one registered model version. Serving loads the alias, so promotion and rollback are just moving it; aliases replace the deprecated registry stages.

modelcard.d: A short document shipped with a model: intended and out-of-scope uses, training data summary, evaluation results by subgroup, limitations, risks and mitigations. Datasheets do this for datasets and system cards for foundation models.

modelgate.d: An automated check a candidate model must pass before promotion: no worse than the champion beyond a tolerance, above absolute floors, above floors on key slices, and within latency and size limits. It returns a failing exit code so CI can block the release.

modelregistry.d: A versioned store of trained models and their metadata, used to promote, roll back and audit what is deployed.

molecule.d: A framework for testing Ansible roles: create a throwaway instance, converge the role, converge again to prove idempotence, then verify the end state.

monkeypatch.d: pytest's built-in fixture for temporarily changing attributes, dictionary items or environment variables during one test; everything is restored automatically afterwards.

mro.d: The order in which Python searches a class and its parents for an attribute, visible as Class.__mro__. super() follows it, so with multiple inheritance a call can reach a sibling class before the parent.

mrr.d: For each query take 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant result (0 if none), then average over queries. It suits tasks where one good hit matters, such as question answering, and ignores everything after the first relevant result.

mrtr.d: The MCP 2026-07-28 pattern replacing server-initiated requests: the server answers with an input-required result listing what it needs, and the client retries the original request with the user's responses and any state token, under a new request id.

mtls.d: TLS where the client also presents a certificate, so both sides authenticate. Common for service-to-service traffic in service meshes and zero-trust networks; it needs automated issuance, rotation and revocation of many short-lived certificates.

mttr.d: The average time from the start of an incident to restoration of normal service. Tracked across incidents to see whether detection and response are improving.

multistage.d: A Dockerfile that uses several FROM stages so build tools and dev dependencies stay in an early stage and only runtime files are copied into the final image. Smaller and safer.

mutability.d: Immutable values (numbers, strings, tuples) cannot change in place; mutable ones (lists, dictionaries, objects) can. Two names can refer to the same mutable object, so changing one changes the other, a source of aliasing bugs. Copy deliberately.

mutabledefault.d: A bug where def f(x, items=[]) shares one list across calls, because defaults are evaluated once at definition time. Use None as the default and create the list inside the function.

mutationtest.d: Deliberately introducing small bugs (flip a comparison, delete a line) and checking whether the test suite fails. Surviving mutants reveal tests that run code without asserting its behavior; a more honest measure than line coverage.

mutex.d: Synchronization primitives. A mutex lets one thread at a time into a critical section; a semaphore is a counter allowing up to N holders (pools, rate limits). Misuse causes deadlock, so acquire locks in a consistent order and hold them briefly.

mvcc.d: Multiversion concurrency control: updates create new row versions so readers and writers do not block each other.

mypy.d: The reference static type checker for Python. It reads your annotations, reports mismatches before the program runs, and has a strict mode (strict = true) for new code.

nacl.d: A stateless subnet-level firewall with allow and deny rules evaluated in order.

naivedt.d: A naive datetime has no time zone; an aware one does, and comparing the two raises TypeError. Store and compute in UTC (datetime.now(timezone.utc)) and convert with zoneinfo only for display.

namemain.d: A guard that runs code only when a file is executed directly, not when it is imported. It lets one file serve as both a reusable module and a script, and pairs with a main() function that returns an exit code.

narrowing.d: How TypeScript refines a union type inside a branch using typeof, in, instanceof, equality checks or custom type guards, so each branch sees the precise type.

natgw.d: A managed service that lets private subnets reach the internet without being reachable from it; billed per hour and per GB.

ndarray.d: A fixed-type, fixed-size block of numbers in memory with a shape. Whole-array operations run in compiled loops, which is why arrays are tens to hundreds of times faster than Python loops for numeric work.

ndcg.d: Normalized discounted cumulative gain: a metric scoring a ranking against graded relevance labels, rewarding good results near the top. Pair a judgment list of important queries with nDCG and A/B tests to tune relevance with evidence instead of impressions.

networkpolicy.d: A Kubernetes rule limiting which Pods can talk to which. Without one, every Pod can reach every Pod; start with default-deny and allow required flows (needs a CNI that enforces it).

nextfunction.d: Each middleware must do exactly one of: send a response, call next() to pass on, or call next(err) to jump to error handlers. Doing none hangs the request; doing two causes 'headers already sent'.

nextpublic.d: Environment variables with this prefix are inlined into the browser bundle, so they must never contain secrets.

nexttick.d: Schedules a callback to run right after the current operation, before promise callbacks and before the loop moves on.

nistairmf.d: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology's voluntary AI Risk Management Framework, organized as Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, with a generative AI profile. ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable AI management system standard.

nodemodules.d: The folder where installed packages live. Node resolves bare imports by searching it and each parent folder. Never commit it; rebuild it with npm ci.

nodestream.d: An interface for processing data in chunks as it flows, keeping memory use low for large inputs and outputs.

nodetest.d: Node.js's built-in test runner with describe/it, hooks, mocks, fake timers, reporters and coverage, plus node:assert. node --test discovers *.test.mjs files, runs each file in its own process and exits 1 on failure.

normaldist.d: The bell curve defined by mean and standard deviation: about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation, 95% within two. By the central limit theorem, averages of many independent values approach it, and the standard error of a mean shrinks as 1 over the square root of n.

normalization.d: Organizing tables so each fact is stored once, which reduces duplication and update errors.

normlayer.d: Layers that keep activations in a stable range so deep networks train: BatchNorm normalizes each feature across the batch (common in CNNs); LayerNorm and RMSNorm normalize within each example (standard in transformers).

npaxis.d: The dimension an operation collapses. In a 2-D array axis=0 runs down the rows (one result per column) and axis=1 across the columns (one result per row): the axis you name disappears.

npm.d: Node's package manager and the public registry of JavaScript packages: installs dependencies, runs scripts and publishes packages. pnpm, Yarn and Bun follow the same model.

nsg.d: Azure firewall rules that allow or deny traffic by port, protocol and source for subnets or network interfaces.

nuget.d: The .NET package manager and public feed. Apply supply-chain habits: pin versions, use lock files and central package management, review new dependencies and scan with dotnet list package --vulnerable.

null3.d: A marker for unknown or missing data. Comparisons with NULL are neither true nor false, so use IS NULL.

nullablereftypes.d: A compile-time check: with <Nullable>enable</Nullable>, string means never null and string? means may be null, and the compiler warns where a possible null is dereferenced. Treat warnings as errors in serious projects.

oauth.d: A framework that lets an app obtain limited access to a user's data at another service via tokens, without handling the user's password. It delegates authorization; it does not by itself prove identity.

observerpattern.d: Subscribers are notified when a subject changes. Event emitters, UI state stores and message brokers are this idea at different scales. Risks: hidden control flow and memory leaks from forgotten unsubscribes.

obsspan.d: One timed step inside a trace, such as a database query or an LLM call; spans nest to form the full request path.

oidc.d: An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds an ID token and standard claims, so apps can learn who signed in. It powers 'Sign in with Google' and enterprise SSO.

oidcfed.d: Letting an external identity, like a GitHub Actions job, assume a cloud role through a trust relationship so no static keys are stored.

onlineeval.d: Scoring live traffic: automatic checks on every response, sampled model-graded review, user feedback and business outcomes. Catches drift and new failure types that a fixed offline dataset cannot, and feeds failures back into the test set.

oomkiller.d: The Linux kernel's last resort when memory is exhausted: it kills a process to survive. In containers a cgroup memory limit triggers the same, shown as SIGKILL and exit code 137. Investigate leaks, unbounded caches, limits and worker counts rather than retrying.

openapi.d: A machine-readable format for describing HTTP APIs (paths, schemas, auth, errors). It drives docs, validation, mock servers and generated clients and SDKs.

opencost.d: A CNCF project that allocates Kubernetes node, storage and network cost to namespaces, labels and workloads from resource requests and usage. The biggest lever it exposes is requests far above actual use.

opentofu.d: The open-source, Linux Foundation fork of Terraform created after the 2023 license change. Same HCL and workflow; the CLI command is tofu.

optionspattern.d: Binds a configuration section (appsettings.json, environment variables, command line) to a typed class and injects it as IOptions<T>. Secrets: dotnet user-secrets locally, environment variables or a vault in production.

orchestratorworker.d: A workflow where a central model breaks a task into sub-tasks and delegates them to worker calls or sub-agents, then combines the results. Useful when sub-tasks cannot be known in advance; costs more tokens and needs good handoffs.

otel.d: A vendor-neutral standard and set of SDKs for emitting traces, metrics and logs.

outbox.d: Write an event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the state change, then have a separate relay publish it to the broker. It avoids the dual-write problem: you never record a change without its event, or the reverse. Consumers must still be idempotent.

outlier.d: A value far from the rest. It may be an error (a typo, a unit mix-up) or the most interesting case (fraud, best customer). Remove only what is provably wrong; otherwise keep, cap or transform.

outputencoding.d: Converting data into a safe form for the place it is written (HTML text, attribute, URL, JavaScript, CSS). Template engines escape HTML by default; a javascript: URL in an href still needs a scheme check.

outputhandling.d: OWASP LLM05: using model output without validation in a browser, shell, SQL or another system. Treat output as untrusted input: validate against a schema and escape for the target.

overfitting.d: When a model memorizes training noise and performs worse on new data than on the data it learned from.

owasp.d: A non-profit community that publishes free application security standards and tools, including the Top 10, ASVS and the cheat sheet series.

owaspllm.d: OWASP's 2025 ranking of the ten most critical risks in LLM applications, from LLM01 Prompt Injection to LLM10 Unbounded Consumption.

owasptop10.d: A consensus ranking of the ten most critical web application security risks, used as shared vocabulary for reviews, audits and training. The 2025 edition added supply chain failures and exceptional-condition handling.

paas.d: Running your code or data on managed platforms where the provider handles servers, patching and scaling.

packagejson.d: A project's manifest: name, version, type, scripts, dependencies, devDependencies, engines, exports. Commit it together with the lockfile.

pagecache.d: RAM the kernel uses to cache file data so repeated reads run at memory speed. It is why free memory looks low on a healthy Linux host (check available instead). Writes land here first, so durability needs fsync, which databases call on commit.

pagedattention.d: A way to store the KV cache in fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, like virtual-memory pages, instead of one contiguous slab per sequence. It removes most fragmentation and waste, so engines like vLLM fit larger batches.

pairwisecomparison.d: Asking a judge which of two outputs is better instead of scoring each alone. Easier for judges than absolute scores but sensitive to position and length bias, so run each pair in both orders and count only agreeing verdicts.

paralleltoolcalls.d: A single model response containing several tool requests that can run together. The application must answer every one with a matching tool result in the next message; an unanswered call is rejected or confuses the model.

parameterizedquery.d: SQL sent with placeholders (?, $1, %s) and the values sent separately, so the database treats values as data whatever characters they contain. The reliable fix for SQL injection; table names and ORDER BY still need an allow-list.

parametrize.d: Runs one test body over several input sets and reports each as its own test; ids= gives readable names.

paramquery.d: A query where SQL text and values are sent separately, so input can never be parsed as SQL. In node-postgres, write $1 placeholders and pass values in an array.

parentdocument.d: Matching on small, precise chunks but returning the larger parent section (or the neighbouring chunks) to the model, combining sharp matching with enough surrounding context to be understood.

parquet.d: A columnar, compressed file format. Data is split into row groups with min/max statistics, so engines read only needed columns and skip data that cannot match a filter (predicate pushdown); partitioned folders let whole directories be skipped.

partial.d: An index built only over rows matching a condition, which keeps it small and fast.

partitionkey.d: The attribute that decides which storage partition holds an item. Queries must supply it, and uneven values create hot partitions.

passatk.d: The probability that at least one of k sampled attempts passes a check, widely used for code generation where any correct sample counts. Differs from the average pass rate of single attempts and rises with k.

passkey.d: A passwordless credential: a per-site key pair where the private key stays on the device or in a synced credential manager and signs a challenge after a local unlock. Bound to the real domain, so it resists phishing.

pathenv.d: An environment variable listing folders the shell searches, left to right, when you type a command name without a slash. The first match wins, which is why a program in the current folder needs ./ in front.

pathlib.d: The standard module that models filesystem paths as objects: Path("a") / "b.json", .read_text(), .mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True), .glob(). It replaces most string and os.path juggling; pass encoding="utf-8" for text.

pathtoregexp.d: The library that turns Express route strings like /users/:id into matchers. Express 5 uses version 8: wildcards must be named (/files/*splat) and some regex characters in strings are no longer supported.

pathtraversal.d: A file name such as ../secret.txt that walks out of the intended folder. Fix: resolve the final path and check it is still inside the folder, or avoid user-chosen paths by mapping generated IDs to stored files.

pdb.d: A Kubernetes object that limits how many replicas of an application can be voluntarily evicted at once (drains, upgrades, autoscaler scale-down) so a minimum stays available. It does not protect against involuntary failures such as a node crash.

peft.d: A family of methods (LoRA, prefix tuning, adapters) that freeze the base model and train a small number of extra parameters. Training memory drops sharply and the result is a small adapter file you can swap per task; Hugging Face's peft library implements them.

percentile.d: The latency under which a given share of requests finish; p99 is the slowest 1% boundary. Averages hide tail latency that users feel.

perceptron.d: A threshold neuron that nudges its weights after each mistake. It learns any linearly separable rule (AND, OR) but can never solve XOR, because one neuron draws only one straight line.

perfbudget.d: Explicit limits on metrics or sizes, such as LCP under 2.5 s or a maximum JavaScript size per route, enforced in CI with tools like Lighthouse CI and confirmed with real user monitoring, so performance cannot silently regress.

persistedquery.d: Registering GraphQL queries ahead of time and sending only a hash, often by GET. It enables CDN caching and, as an allowlist, blocks arbitrary expensive queries.

pgchanges.d: Realtime feature that streams inserts, updates and deletes from tables in the supabase_realtime publication, filtered by RLS.

pgqueue.d: Using a database table as a queue with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so workers claim distinct rows. Its big advantage is enqueuing in the same transaction as the business write, avoiding dual writes. Libraries: pg-boss, Graphile Worker, River.

pgstat.d: A Postgres extension that tracks execution counts and timings for every distinct query.

pgvector.d: A Postgres extension that adds a vector column type, distance operators and approximate indexes for similarity search.

pinball.d: The loss minimized by a quantile forecast: for quantile q, under-predictions are weighted by q and over-predictions by 1 - q. Training or scoring at several quantiles (for example 0.1, 0.5, 0.9) yields prediction intervals, whose empirical coverage should be checked.

pipelining.d: Sending many Redis commands without waiting for each reply, to cut network round trips (typically 0.2 to 1 ms each in a data center). It improves throughput but is not atomic; use MULTI/EXEC or a Lua script when atomicity is needed.

pk.d: A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL.

pkce.d: An OAuth extension where the client sends a hash (code challenge) at the start and the matching secret (code verifier) when redeeming the code. A stolen authorization code is then useless to an attacker.

pkgmanager.d: Tools that install dependencies reproducibly: npm, pnpm, pip, uv, poetry, cargo. A lockfile pins exact versions; review new dependencies, because AI assistants can suggest nonexistent or typosquatted package names.

planner.d: The part of the database that estimates costs and chooses how to execute a query.

playbook.d: A YAML file of plays, each mapping a group of hosts to tasks and roles. Run it with ansible-playbook, ideally previewed first with --check --diff.

playwright.d: A browser automation and end-to-end testing library for Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. Actions auto-wait, locators favor roles and visible text (getByRole), and the trace viewer replays failed CI runs step by step.

policy.d: A rule attached to a table that decides which rows a role may SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE.

policyascode.d: Encoding rules such as no public buckets or required tags as tests that run on the plan in CI and block violating changes before they are applied.

pooling.d: Shrinks a feature map by keeping the strongest (max) or average value in each block, cutting data and giving a little tolerance to small shifts. It does not provide full translation invariance.

popularitybias.d: Models trained on logged clicks over-recommend already popular items, which then collect more clicks and crowd out the long tail; top slots also get clicks simply for being on top. Mitigations include exploration, logging positions, propensity weighting and diversity-aware re-ranking.

portcheck.d: Tools for seeing which process owns which port or file: ss -tulpn lists listening sockets with their processes, lsof -i :3000 finds who holds a port, and lsof +L1 finds deleted files still held open. Connection refused means nothing is listening; a timeout suggests a firewall.

positionbias.d: The tendency of model judges to favour the answer shown first (or the longer one) regardless of quality. Detect it by swapping the order and measuring how often the verdict flips, and neutralise it by counting only order-independent verdicts.

postgrest.d: The service that turns your Postgres schema into a REST API. It runs queries as the caller's database role.

postmortem.d: A written review after an incident covering timeline, impact, root causes and tracked action items, without blaming individuals. It asks how the system allowed the failure.

ppr.d: Serving a static shell instantly and streaming dynamic parts into it; the model behind Next.js 16 Cache Components.

precisionrecall.d: Precision, recall and F1: share of flagged items that are right, share of true items found, and their harmonic mean.

precommit.d: Checks that run automatically before each commit (format, lint, secret scan), managed by tools such as pre-commit or Husky. CI repeats them on a clean machine so they cannot be skipped and nothing depends on one laptop.

predictionlogging.d: Recording each prediction with a request id, entity id, timestamp, model version, the transformed features and the score, so drift checks, debugging and later label joins are possible. Sample at high volume and treat the logs as personal data.

prefill.d: The two phases of LLM inference. Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel and builds the KV cache (compute-bound, sets time to first token); decode generates one token per step by reading weights and cache (memory-bound, sets streaming speed). Chunked prefill interleaves slices of long prompts with decode so others do not stall.

prefixcaching.d: Reusing the cached KV blocks of a prompt prefix shared across requests (system prompt, few-shot examples, a document). It cuts prefill work and latency, and is why stable content should come first in a prompt.

preflight.d: An OPTIONS request the browser sends before a non-simple cross-origin request (custom header, JSON content type, PUT/DELETE). If the server does not consent, the real request is never sent. Max-Age caches the answer.

presence.d: Realtime feature that tracks which clients are online and shares small pieces of state between them.

pretraining.d: The first training stage: predicting the next token across a huge text corpus to learn language and world knowledge.

preventdestroy.d: A Terraform lifecycle setting that makes any plan fail if it would destroy the resource. Use it on databases, buckets and other stateful resources.

previewdeploy.d: A deployment created for each non-production branch or pull request, with its own URL for review and testing.

printdebugging.d: Printing values to see what really happened. In Python, f"{x=}" shows the expression and its value and !r shows invisible differences. For code that stays, use the logging module with levels.

privateendpoint.d: A private IP inside your VNet for a PaaS service, so its public access can be disabled.

probes.d: Kubernetes health checks: readiness controls whether a Pod receives traffic, liveness decides whether to restart it, startup protects slow boots. Liveness checks should not depend on external services.

problemdetails.d: RFC 9457's standard JSON error format for HTTP APIs: type, title, status, detail and instance, plus extension fields such as field errors or a trace id. It replaced RFC 7807.

process.d: A running program with its own virtual address space, file descriptors, environment and PID. Created by fork and exec, isolated from other processes, and reaped by its parent when it exits (otherwise it lingers as a zombie).

procfs.d: A virtual filesystem where the Linux kernel exposes live process and system data as files: /proc/PID/status, /proc/PID/limits, /proc/meminfo and more. Tools such as ps, top and lsof read it, and you can too.

producersacks.d: The producer setting for how many replicas must confirm a write: 0 (none), 1 (leader), all (every in-sync replica). Combine acks=all with replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2 and the idempotent producer (no duplicates or reordering on retry).

productquantization.d: A compression method that splits each vector into sub-vectors and replaces each with the id of its nearest entry in a small learned codebook, shrinking memory by an order of magnitude. Distances become approximate, so systems often rerank the top candidates with the full vectors.

promise.d: An object standing for a value that is not ready yet. It is pending, then settles once as fulfilled (with a value) or rejected (with an error). Handlers chain, and one .catch handles an error from any earlier step.

promiseall.d: Combinators for several promises: all (wait for all, reject on the first failure), allSettled (report every outcome), race (first to settle), any (first success). They run work concurrently, not one after another.

promptcaching.d: Reusing the processed form of a long, unchanged prompt prefix across calls, to cut latency and cost.

promptchaining.d: Splitting a task into a fixed sequence of model calls where each output feeds the next (extract, then classify, then draft). More predictable and easier to test than one giant prompt or a free-running agent, at the cost of extra calls and latency.

promptinjection.d: An attack where instructions hidden in user input or retrieved content hijack a model's behavior. Mitigate by limiting what the model can do.

promptleak.d: OWASP LLM07: the hidden instructions or embedded secrets of an app being revealed to users or attackers. Assume the system prompt can be extracted and keep secrets and enforcement in code.

promptversioning.d: Treating prompts as versioned artifacts: stored in files or a prompt-management tool, identified by version or content hash, logged with every model call and tested before release, so a change in quality or cost can be traced to a specific edit and rolled back.

propertytest.d: Stating a rule that must hold for all inputs (decode(encode(x)) == x) and letting a tool generate many cases, then shrink a failure to a minimal example. Hypothesis (Python) and fast-check (TypeScript) are the common tools.

protobuf.d: A language-neutral schema and binary serialization format used by gRPC. Fields are identified by number, so numbers must never be reused and removed ones should be reserved.

protocol.d: A typing construct that describes the methods an argument must have, without requiring inheritance. It lets production code accept any matching object and tests pass a simple fake.

proxyts.d: The Next.js 16 file that replaced middleware.ts; it runs before requests on the Node.js runtime.

psi.d: A drift score that bins a feature using the reference data and sums (current share minus reference share) times the log of their ratio across bins. A common rule of thumb reads below 0.1 as stable, 0.1 to 0.25 as moderate and above 0.25 as large, but these cut-offs are conventions, not laws.

publishablekey.d: The low-privilege Supabase API key meant for browsers and apps; RLS policies decide what it can access. It replaces the legacy anon key.

pulumi.d: An infrastructure-as-code tool where you write infrastructure in a general-purpose language such as TypeScript or Python, with real loops, functions and unit tests, while keeping the same state and plan model as Terraform. AWS CDK is a related approach that generates CloudFormation.

purefn.d: A pure function returns the same output for the same input and changes nothing outside itself. Side effects are writes to files, globals, databases or the screen. Pure functions are easy to test and reason about, so isolate side effects at the edges.

pvalue.d: The probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis (no effect) were true. It is not the probability the hypothesis is true, nor the effect size. Report effect sizes and intervals, and beware multiple comparisons.

pvc.d: A Pod's request for storage of a given size and class. A StorageClass and CSI driver provision the actual disk (EBS, Azure Disk); the disk is usually bound to one availability zone, which constrains where the Pod can run.

pwhash.d: Storing a one-way, slow, salted hash of each password instead of the password. Fast hashes such as SHA-256 are unsuitable because attackers can test billions of guesses per second.

pyclass.d: A class is a blueprint and an instance is one object built from it; self is the instance inside methods. Attributes set in the class body are shared by all instances, so mutable ones there are a common trap.

pydantic.d: A Python library that defines data shapes as typed classes and validates or parses input against them, with clear errors. In LLM apps it supplies the schema (model_json_schema) and validates model output; FastAPI is built on it.

pyenum.d: A fixed set of named values (Status.PAID) that replaces magic strings and numbers, so typos fail early and tools can check exhaustiveness. StrEnum and IntEnum members also behave like strings and ints.

pyfixture.d: A function marked @pytest.fixture whose return or yielded value is injected into tests by parameter name. Code after yield is teardown; scope sets how often it is rebuilt; conftest.py shares fixtures across a directory.

pylogging.d: The standard module for event logging: create a logger per module with getLogger(__name__), choose a level, and configure handlers and format once in the application. Pass values as arguments and use log.exception inside except to capture tracebacks.

pymodule.d: A module is a .py file; a package is a directory of modules (traditionally with __init__.py). import makes their names available, and circular imports or files named like libraries are common sources of confusing errors.

pyproject.d: The standard project file: metadata and dependencies in [project], the build backend in [build-system], dev-only dependencies in [dependency-groups], and tool settings in [tool.*] tables. It replaces setup.py and scattered requirements files.

pyproperty.d: A decorator that exposes a method as an attribute (order.total), so callers do not care whether the value is stored or computed. Keep properties cheap and free of side effects.

pyright.d: Microsoft's fast Python type checker, also the engine behind Pylance in VS Code, with off, basic, standard and strict modes.

pytest.d: Python's most popular test framework: plain assert statements, fixtures for setup and teardown, parametrize to run one test over many inputs, and plugins such as pytest-asyncio, pytest-cov and pytest-xdist.

pytypehints.d: Optional annotations such as def f(x: int) -> str that document intent and let tools like mypy or pyright find errors before running. Python itself does not enforce them at run time; libraries like Pydantic can.

qlora.d: LoRA training on top of a base model frozen in 4-bit NF4 precision, with the adapters kept in higher precision. It lets a model of several billion parameters be fine-tuned on a single mid-range GPU, at some cost in training speed.

qosclass.d: A Pod's priority for survival under node resource pressure, derived from its requests and limits: Guaranteed (requests equal limits), Burstable (some set) and BestEffort (none). BestEffort Pods are evicted first.

quantization.d: Storing model weights (and sometimes activations or the KV cache) in fewer bits, such as 8-bit or 4-bit, to cut memory and memory traffic. Methods like GPTQ and AWQ quantize after training; quantization-aware training trains with rounding in the loop. Always evaluate quality on your own task.

queryrewriting.d: Transforming the user's query before retrieval: resolving pronouns from the conversation, expanding abbreviations, splitting a compound question into sub-queries or generating variants. Use only where measurements show gains, since each rewrite adds latency and can change intent.

rabbitmq.d: An AMQP message broker with flexible routing: producers publish to exchanges, bindings route to queues. Quorum queues replicate with Raft; classic queue mirroring was removed in 4.0. Supports acks, prefetch, publisher confirms, TTLs and dead-letter exchanges.

racecondition.d: A bug whose outcome depends on timing, such as two threads doing counter += 1 (read, add, write) and losing an update. Fix with locks, atomic operations, immutable data or message passing; correctness must not depend on luck.

rag.d: Retrieval-augmented generation: fetch relevant documents first, then give them to an LLM to answer from.

ratelimit.d: Capping how many requests a client can make in a time window to prevent abuse and overload.

rdbaof.d: Redis durability options: RDB writes periodic point-in-time snapshots (fast restart, can lose recent writes); AOF logs every write command (with fsync every second, at most about a second is lost). Neither equals a database with synchronous replication.

rds.d: AWS's managed relational databases (Postgres, MySQL and others) with backups, patching and Multi-AZ failover.

reactcompiler.d: A build-time tool, stable at 1.0 since October 2025, that analyzes components and hooks and inserts memoization automatically, making most manual useMemo, useCallback and memo unnecessary.

reactkey.d: A stable, unique identifier React uses to match list items between renders. Use a data id, not the array index, or state can attach to the wrong row.

reactpattern.d: An agent pattern in which the model alternates between reasoning about what to do and acting through a tool, then reads the observation and continues. The basic shape behind most tool-using loops.

readreplica.d: A copy of a database that serves reads while the primary takes writes. It scales read-heavy workloads, but replication lag means a read right after a write can be stale, so read your own writes from the primary when it matters.

realtime.d: Supabase's WebSocket service for live database changes, broadcast messages and presence.

reasoningmodel.d: Models trained to think through intermediate steps before answering, improving results on hard multi-step problems at a cost in tokens and latency.

rebase.d: Replaying your commits on top of another base commit to produce a linear history. Safe on local, unshared commits; use --force-with-lease when pushing afterward.

rebasemerge.d: Merge joins histories, creating a merge commit unless it can fast-forward. Rebase replays your commits onto a new base, creating new commits and a linear history. Rebase only unpublished commits; squash merge collapses a branch into one commit.

recallk.d: The fraction of questions where a relevant passage appears in the top k retrieved results.

receptivefield.d: The patch of the original image that can influence one unit. Deeper layers have larger receptive fields, which is how small local detectors combine into whole-object understanding.

reconciliation.d: React's process of diffing the newly rendered UI description against the previous one and applying only the differences to the DOM.

reconciliationjob.d: A periodic job that lists resources or events from the source API and repairs gaps left by missed or failed webhooks. The webhook is a hint; the API is the truth.

reconciliationloop.d: The pattern where a controller repeatedly compares desired state with actual state and acts to close the gap. Kubernetes controllers, Argo CD and Flux all work this way, which is why they repair drift without being told.

recursion.d: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version, with a base case that stops it. Natural for trees and divide-and-conquer; each call uses stack space, so very deep recursion overflows and an iterative loop may be better.

redirecturi.d: The registered callback URL where the identity provider sends the user and the authorization code. It must be matched exactly; wildcard matching enables code theft through open redirects.

redis.d: An in-memory data structure server: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams and more, with atomic commands executed one at a time. Used for caching, sessions, rate limiting, queues and leaderboards; not a replacement for a durable primary database.

rediscluster.d: Sharding across nodes using 16,384 hash slots (CRC16 of the key mod 16384), each owned by a primary with replicas. Multi-key commands need keys in one slot, which hash tags such as {user:42} guarantee. Sentinel is the separate high-availability option for a single primary.

redisstream.d: An append-only log inside Redis with entry ids, consumer groups, per-consumer pending lists and acknowledgements (XACK), and reclaiming of stuck messages (XAUTOCLAIM). At-least-once and durable-ish, unlike fire-and-forget Pub/Sub; Kafka suits much larger, longer-retained flows.

redos.d: A pattern with nested quantifiers such as (a+)+$ can take exponential time on a crafted input and freeze a worker. Avoid nested quantifiers, cap input length, use a linear-time engine for untrusted input.

redteam.d: Structured adversarial testing of an AI system to elicit harmful, private, biased or policy-violating behavior, including prompt injection and tool misuse. Make the cases a regression suite that grows from real incidents and runs on every change.

refactoring.d: Improving the structure of code without changing its behavior, backed by tests. Typical targets are code smells: duplicated blocks, giant functions, deep nesting (use early returns), unclear names and magic numbers.

reflog.d: A local log of where HEAD and branches pointed over time. After a bad reset, rebase or deleted branch, git reflog shows the old commit ids so you can restore them; unreachable commits survive for weeks before garbage collection.

refreshinterval.d: New documents become searchable after the next refresh (every second by default), not instantly. Segments are immutable, updates are delete plus add, and merges run in the background; a translog gives durability. Relax refresh during bulk loads.

refreshtoken.d: A long-lived credential used to get a new access token. Supabase refresh tokens are single-use.

regex.d: A compact pattern language for text, used in Python through the re module: use raw strings, compile reused patterns, prefer re.fullmatch for validation, and avoid regex for nested formats like HTML. Catastrophic backtracking on hostile input can freeze a service.

regexgroups.d: Parentheses in a pattern remember the part they match. Named groups ((?P<date>...) in Python) let code read m['date'] instead of a numbered index, so adding a field does not shift every index.

regressiontest.d: A test that fails before a bug fix and passes after, written for each fixed bug so it cannot quietly return. Write it first and confirm it fails for the right reason.

relationaldb.d: A database that stores data in tables of rows and typed columns, links tables with keys, and is queried with SQL. Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server.

releasetracking.d: Tagging errors and traces with the deployed version so you can see which release introduced a problem.

relpath.d: An absolute path starts at the root (/home/ada/notes/a.txt); a relative path starts at the working directory (notes/a.txt). . means here, .. the parent folder, ~ your home folder.

replayprotection.d: Defending against reuse of a captured valid request by including a timestamp in the signed content, rejecting old ones, and deduplicating by event id.

repositorypattern.d: An interface for loading and saving domain objects (orders.get(id), orders.save(order)) that hides the database from business logic and gives tests an in-memory fake. Valuable with real domain rules; unnecessary ceremony for thin CRUD.

reproducibility.d: The ability to rebuild a model from its recorded code version, data version, dependencies, config and seeds. It usually means the same result within noise, since some GPU kernels are nondeterministic.

reqlimits.d: Requests are the CPU and memory the scheduler reserves for a container; limits are the ceiling. Exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOM-killed, while CPU limits throttle.

reranker.d: A second-stage model that reorders retrieved candidates by how well each answers the question.

resourcegroup.d: A container for related Azure resources that share a lifecycle and can be managed and permissioned together.

resourcehints.d: Tags that tell the browser what it will need: preconnect opens a connection early, preload fetches a known critical resource now, prefetch fetches a likely next page at low priority, fetchpriority raises or lowers a request's priority. Overuse backfires.

rest.d: A style for HTTP APIs: URLs name resources (nouns like /notes/2), standard methods act on them, and responses are representations such as JSON. Most 'REST APIs' follow it loosely, so predictability matters more than purity.

resulttype.d: Handling failure as a returned value instead of a thrown exception: Go returns (value, error), Rust returns Result<T, E> and Option<T> with the ? operator. Control flow is explicit, and the compiler or linters push you to handle every case.
resulttype.n: Result type and errors as values

retrievalacl.d: Enforcing who may see which chunks as a filter inside the retrieval query (on metadata such as tenant, group or classification), so unauthorised text is never retrieved and cannot leak through the prompt. Instructions in the prompt are not access control.

retryafter.d: On 429 or overload, wait the time the server's retry-after header gives, otherwise back off exponentially with jitter, and cap attempts. Never retry 400 or 401, which fail identically every time.

retryvalidate.d: Parsing model output against a schema and, on failure, sending the validation error back to the model for a corrected attempt, up to a small limit. It catches problems decoding constraints cannot, such as out-of-range values or unknown ids.

rightsizing.d: Matching provisioned capacity to observed need by comparing CPU, memory and I/O over weeks and moving to smaller or newer resource types. Do it before buying commitments.

rlhf.d: Training a model toward responses that people or AI judges prefer, to make it more helpful and safer.

rls.d: A Postgres feature that filters which rows each query may read or change, using policies attached to the table.

rocauc.d: Threshold-free ranking metrics. ROC AUC is the chance a random positive outranks a random negative; PR AUC (average precision) tracks precision against recall and is more informative when positives are rare.

roleassignment.d: The binding of who (principal), what (role) and where (scope) in Azure RBAC.

roleprompting.d: Setting a role in the system prompt (for example a support assistant for a named product) to focus vocabulary, tone and priorities. A role helps but does not replace explicit rules, and it is not a security boundary.

routehandler.d: A route.ts file that defines an HTTP endpoint in the App Router, such as a webhook or public JSON API.

rowlock.d: A lock on specific rows that stops other transactions from changing them until commit.

rpo.d: How much recent data you can afford to lose, measured as time between the last good copy and the failure.

rrf.d: A method for merging ranked lists by summing 1 divided by (k plus rank) for each document, with no need for comparable scores.

rto.d: How long a service may be down after a failure before the business is harmed.

rubric.d: A specific written description of what earns each score, used by human or model graders (for example: every factual claim must be supported by the sources, else 0). Binary or three-point scales with concrete criteria are more consistent than vague 1-to-10 scores.

rugpull.d: An attack in which a server changes a tool's description or behaviour after the user approved it, so hidden instructions reach the model later. Defend by fingerprinting approved tool definitions, reviewing diffs and re-asking approval on change.

rulesfile.d: A repository file that coding agents read automatically: commands to build and test, architecture notes, conventions and never-do rules. AGENTS.md is an emerging cross-tool convention; others use CLAUDE.md or editor-specific rules. Keep it short and current.

rum.d: Measuring performance in real sessions (for example with the web-vitals library) across devices, networks and countries. Field data, including the public CrUX dataset, is the source of truth; lab tools such as Lighthouse diagnose and gate pull requests.

runbook.d: A step-by-step document for a specific scenario, such as a leaked cloud key or a compromised account, listing signals, containment steps, owners and where the logs are.

rustownership.d: Rust's compile-time memory model: each value has one owner and is freed when it goes out of scope; references borrow it, and the borrow checker forbids use after free, double free and data races in safe code, with no garbage collector.

s3.d: AWS's object storage: highly durable buckets of files addressed by key, with storage classes and lifecycle rules.

safetensors.d: A model weight file format that stores only tensors and cannot execute code on load, unlike pickle-based checkpoints. Preferred for sharing and downloading models; also pair with torch.load(weights_only=True) for older files.

sameorigin.d: Page JavaScript may read responses only from its own origin (scheme + host + port). localhost:9100 and localhost:9101 are different origins but the same site; localhost and 127.0.0.1 are different sites. CORS opts in to reads.

samesite.d: A cookie attribute controlling whether the browser sends the cookie on cross-site requests. Lax blocks it on cross-site POSTs and removes most CSRF risk by default.

samplingnoise.d: Random wobble in an observed rate or mean because of a limited sample. A rate near 26% from 250 rows varies by about 3 points either way, so small gaps between groups may be chance.

sas.d: A signed URL token granting limited, time-bound access to storage; prefer user delegation SAS signed with Entra credentials.

satisfies.d: A TypeScript operator that checks a value against a type without widening its inferred type, giving validation and precise literal inference together.

savingsplan.d: Pricing options: commit to steady usage for a discount (Savings Plans, reservations), or use spare capacity cheaply with interruptions (Spot).

sbom.d: A machine-readable inventory of every component inside a build, in CycloneDX or SPDX format. It lets you answer 'which of our services use this vulnerable version?' within minutes.

scd2.d: A dimension whose attributes change over time. Type 2 keeps history by closing the old row (valid-to date) and inserting a new one, so reports about the past still show the customer's old country or plan.

schemaregistry.d: A service storing Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema definitions for event topics and enforcing compatibility rules (backward, forward, full) so a producer change cannot break consumers. Treat event schemas as versioned public APIs.

scope.d: Scope decides where a name is visible: a variable created inside a function exists only there. A closure is a function that remembers the variables from where it was created, which is how callbacks, decorators and factory functions keep state.

scp.d: An AWS Organizations guardrail that sets the maximum permissions accounts can ever use, whatever their IAM policies say.

sealedsecrets.d: A Kubernetes controller that decrypts SealedSecret objects, encrypted with the cluster's public key, into ordinary Secrets so the ciphertext can live safely in Git. The ciphertext is tied to that cluster's key, which must be backed up.

searchafter.d: Deep or stable result paging in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch: sort by a tiebreaker-inclusive key and pass the last hit's sort values as search_after, usually with a point in time (PIT). from plus size is capped at 10,000 hits by default and costly deep in results.

seasonalnaive.d: Predict that the next value equals the value one season ago (same weekday last week, same month last year). It is the baseline every forecasting model must beat and the scale used by MASE.

secgroup.d: A stateful firewall attached to a resource. It has allow rules only and can reference other security groups.

secretkey.d: The server-only Supabase API key that bypasses RLS through the service_role role. Never ship it to a browser.

secretscanning.d: Automatically searching code, history and CI logs for committed credentials, as a pre-commit hook and in CI. GitHub push protection blocks known secret formats before they are pushed.

secretsmanager.d: A service that stores credentials encrypted, controls access by identity, audits reads and can rotate secrets automatically. Examples are AWS Secrets Manager and Azure Key Vault.

secretsmod.d: The standard module for cryptographically strong randomness: use secrets.token_urlsafe for tokens and reset links, never random, which is predictable. Pair with hmac.compare_digest for constant-time comparison.

securitydefiner.d: A function option that runs with the owner's privileges instead of the caller's. Useful in RLS helpers, risky if search_path is not set.

selectivity.d: The fraction of rows a filter matches. Low selectivity means many matches, so an index helps less.

selfconsistency.d: Sampling several independent answers (often with step-by-step reasoning) and choosing the most common final answer. Improves reliability on reasoning tasks when the answer is short and comparable, at several times the cost.

selfheal.d: Argo CD automated sync options: selfHeal reverts manual changes in the cluster to match Git, and prune deletes resources that were removed from Git. Pair selfHeal with ignoreDifferences for fields owned by an HPA or a webhook.

semantichtml.d: Choosing HTML elements for their meaning (header, nav, main, button, label) instead of generic divs, which gives keyboard support, accessibility and better machine understanding for free.

semver.d: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: patch fixes, minor adds compatibly, major may break. npm ranges: ^1.2.3 means >=1.2.3 <2.0.0, ~1.2.3 means >=1.2.3 <1.3.0, and ^0.2.3 stays below 0.3.0.

sentry.d: An error and performance monitoring platform that groups exceptions into issues, with stack traces, releases and tracing.

seqscan.d: Reading every row of a table in order; fast for small tables or filters that match most rows.

serialization.d: Turning in-memory data into text or bytes to save or send it (json.dumps), and parsing it back (json.loads). Not everything survives: dates, sets and custom objects need an explicit representation.

serveraction.d: A server-side function that forms or client components can call directly; it is a public endpoint, so it must authenticate and validate.

servercomponent.d: A React component that renders only on the server, can be async and read data directly, and sends no component code to the browser.

serverdiscover.d: The MCP method (2026-07-28) by which a server advertises its supported protocol versions, capabilities, optional instructions and cache hints without a handshake or session. Clients may call it first or send requests directly and react to a version error.

servicelifetime.d: How long an injected object lives: singleton (whole app; must be thread-safe), scoped (one per request; right for DbContext), transient (new each time). Injecting a scoped service into a singleton is a classic bug.

sessioncookie.d: A cookie holding an opaque session id for a signed-in user. Set it HttpOnly (no JavaScript access), Secure (HTTPS only) and SameSite, and use the __Host- prefix to bind it to one host.

setimmediate.d: Schedules a callback for the check phase, right after the poll phase of the event loop.

severity.d: A shared scale (SEV1 most severe) that decides who is paged, how fast people respond and who is informed. Defined in advance so nobody argues about it mid-incident.

sft.d: Continuing to train a pretrained model on example prompt-and-response pairs so it imitates the demonstrated behavior. It teaches format, style and task habits more reliably than it teaches new facts, and is usually the first step before any preference tuning.

shadowmode.d: Running a new model on live traffic without acting on its predictions, to compare it safely against the current one.

sharding.d: Splitting one logical dataset across several machines by a key (a user id, a tenant). It scales writes and storage beyond one server, but cross-shard queries, transactions and rebalancing become hard; pick a key with high cardinality and even load.

shardreplica.d: An index is split into primary shards (each a Lucene index) searched in parallel and merged. Replica shards are copies for availability and read capacity. The primary count is fixed at creation; keep shards tens of GB and avoid thousands of tiny ones.
