sharedresp.d: The split of security duties: the provider secures the cloud infrastructure, and you secure your data, identities and configuration.

shebang.d: The first line of a script (#!/usr/bin/env bash) that tells the operating system which interpreter should run the file when you execute it. The file also needs the executable permission (chmod +x).

shellpipe.d: The shell wiring of standard streams: cmd1 | cmd2 feeds stdout into stdin, > and >> write files, 2>&1 merges stderr into stdout, and tee splits output. Each command also returns an exit code (0 means success) that && and || use.

shellquoting.d: After expanding variables and globs, the shell splits text into words on spaces. Double quotes keep one word but allow $var; single quotes turn off all expansion. Always write "$var" unless you want splitting.

showback.d: Showback reports what each team spent without billing them; chargeback actually allocates the cost to their budget. Start with showback until the allocation data is trusted.

sidecar.d: A helper container that runs alongside the app in the same Pod (log shipper, proxy). Kubernetes implements native sidecars as init containers with restartPolicy: Always, so they start before the app and stop after it.

signals.d: Asynchronous messages to a process: SIGTERM (polite shutdown request, catchable), SIGINT (Ctrl+C), SIGHUP (often reload) and SIGKILL (immediate, uncatchable). Services should handle SIGTERM to drain requests and exit cleanly.

signedurl.d: A temporary link that grants access to a private file until it expires.

simplerequest.d: A GET/POST with only safe headers and a form-like content type goes out with no preflight, and the server processes it even if CORS later hides the response. This is why CORS is not a CSRF defence.

simpson.d: A trend present in every subgroup can reverse when groups are combined because group sizes differ. Related traps: confounders, selection bias, survivorship bias and regression to the mean. Correlation is not causation.

skewness.d: A measure of lopsidedness: a few large values pull the mean above the median (right skew, typical of money and durations). One bad value can change skew from 1 to 30. Use medians and log transforms.

skiplocked.d: A locking option that skips rows already locked by others, used to build job queues.

skpipeline.d: A chain of preprocessing steps and a model fitted as one object. Put imputers, scalers and encoders inside it (with ColumnTransformer for per-column treatment) so cross-validation refits them per fold and nothing leaks from validation data.

sla.d: A contractual promise to customers with consequences such as credits. Keep the internal SLO stricter than the SLA.

sli.d: A measured ratio of good events to valid events, such as the share of requests that succeed or finish under 300 ms.

slo.d: A target for an SLI over a time window, for example 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. It defines how much failure is acceptable.

slots.d: A declaration (or dataclass option slots=True) that fixes the attributes an instance may have, removing the per-instance __dict__. It saves memory, speeds attribute access and turns attribute typos into errors.

slsa.d: A framework of build-integrity levels centered on signed provenance saying which source and workflow produced an artifact. Sigstore and cosign sign and verify artifacts using short-lived CI identities instead of stored keys.

snowflakeid.d: A 64-bit, roughly time-ordered identifier made of a timestamp, a machine id and a per-millisecond sequence, generated without a central database. UUIDv7 (RFC 9562) gives a similar time-ordered property in a 128-bit UUID.

softdelete.d: Marking a row as deleted with a timestamp instead of removing it, so it can be recovered or audited.

solid.d: Five object-oriented design heuristics: single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion. Treat them as guidelines for keeping code easy to change and test, not as rules to apply everywhere.

sops.d: A tool that encrypts the values inside YAML, JSON and env files while leaving keys readable, using age, a cloud KMS or other key providers. Flux decrypts SOPS-encrypted manifests natively.

sortedset.d: A Redis set where each member has a score and members stay ordered by it, with logarithmic insert and rank lookups. The tool for leaderboards, sliding-window rate limits, delayed job schedules and time-ordered indexes.

sparsevector.d: A very high-dimensional vector that is mostly zeros, where each dimension is a vocabulary term and the weight says how important it is. Learned sparse models such as SPLADE expand terms with related words, giving keyword-style matching with some semantic reach; pgvector has a sparsevec type.

specdecoding.d: A small draft model (or n-gram lookup) proposes several tokens that the large model verifies in a single pass. When the draft is often right, latency drops without changing the output distribution.

spy.d: A function that behaves like its implementation and records its calls (count, arguments), so a test can check both the result and the interaction. Keep fakes small; verify real side effects, not internals.

sqli.d: Untrusted input becomes part of a SQL statement and changes its meaning, for example turning a lookup into 'return every row'. Fixed by parameterized queries and allowlisting identifiers.

sqlite.d: A small serverless SQL database stored in a single file, embedded in phones, browsers and apps; dynamically typed and ideal for learning, tests and small sites.

sqlnull.d: NULL means unknown or missing. Comparisons with NULL yield unknown (treated as false), so use IS NULL and COALESCE; x NOT IN (list containing NULL) never matches.

sqlview.d: A saved query that behaves like a read-only table and stores no data itself; a materialized view stores its results and must be refreshed.

sqs.d: AWS's fully managed message queue. Standard queues give high throughput and at-least-once delivery; FIFO queues add per-group ordering. Features: visibility timeout, long polling, delay, dead-letter queues via a redrive policy, and integration with SNS, Lambda and ECS.

srclayout.d: A project structure with code in src/package_name/ and tests in tests/, so tests import the installed package rather than the working directory by accident. It is the layout recommended by the packaging guides for libraries.

sre.d: Running production with software engineering: measurable reliability targets, error budgets, automation of toil and blameless postmortems. Originated at Google.

sse.d: A one-way stream of text events from server to browser over plain HTTP, simple and proxy-friendly, and the transport behind many LLM streaming APIs. Compare with WebSockets (full duplex) and long polling; all need heartbeats and graceful connection draining.

ssg.d: Generating pages' HTML at build time and serving the same files to everyone from a CDN.

ssh.d: Secure remote login and tunneling. Use key pairs (ed25519), keep the private key mode 600, disable password login and root login on servers, and use ~/.ssh/config and port forwarding (ssh -L) to reach private services through a bastion host.

ssr.d: Generating a page's HTML on the server for each request, so users see content before JavaScript loads.

ssrf.d: An attack that makes your server fetch a URL the attacker chose, often to reach internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint. Defend with host allowlists, blocked private ranges, no redirects and metadata hardening.

ssrpkg.d: Package that gives server-rendered frameworks cookie-based Supabase sessions. It replaces the old auth-helpers packages.

stagingarea.d: Git's draft of your next commit. git add copies changes into it, git diff --staged shows it, and git commit records it.

staleclosure.d: A handler or effect that keeps reading values from an older render because it closed over them. Fix with the updater form, correct dependencies or useEffectEvent.

standardwebhooks.d: An open convention for webhook delivery: webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature headers, with signatures like v1,base64 computed as HMAC-SHA256 over id.timestamp.body using a whsec_ secret. Receivers should apply a timestamp tolerance, commonly five minutes.

starschema.d: A dimensional model with a central fact table of events or measurements (orders, clicks) joined to dimension tables (customer, product, date). State the grain, meaning what one row represents, because joins at the wrong grain silently multiply rows.

statecrypt.d: OpenTofu's built-in encryption of state and plan files (since 1.7) using AES-GCM with a key from a passphrase, AWS KMS, GCP KMS or OpenBao. Ephemeral resources and write-only attributes complement it by keeping secrets out of state entirely.

statefulset.d: A Kubernetes workload for stateful applications that gives each replica a stable name (db-0, db-1), ordered start-up and its own PersistentVolumeClaim that follows it across restarts.

statelessness.d: Each request carries everything the server needs (credentials, identifiers), so the server remembers nothing between requests. Any instance can answer, which makes scaling out and retrying simple.

staticbinary.d: A single self-contained executable with no runtime to install, produced by Go and Rust (and by native AOT in .NET and others). It cross-compiles for other operating systems, and makes tiny container images and easy deployment.

stationarity.d: A series is (weakly) stationary if its mean, variance and autocorrelation do not change over time. ARIMA-style models assume it, so trend and seasonality are removed by differencing; tree and neural models handle non-stationarity through features instead.

stdiotransport.d: A local MCP transport where the host launches the server as a process and exchanges messages over standard input and output.

stdstreams.d: Each process has an input stream and two output streams (normal output and errors). > redirects stdout, 2> redirects stderr, 2>&1 merges them, and | connects one command's stdout to the next command's stdin.

steplimit.d: Hard limits enforced by the agent loop in code (steps, tool calls, tokens, money, wall-clock time) that stop a runaway run. They must live in the loop, not in the prompt, because a model can ignore or miscount an instruction.

stopreason.d: Field saying why generation ended: end_turn (finished), max_tokens (truncated), stop_sequence, tool_use (run a tool), pause_turn (continue a server-tool loop), refusal, model_context_window_exceeded. Always branch on it.

storageaccount.d: The top-level Azure Storage resource holding blobs, files, queues and tables under one set of settings.

storageclass.d: S3 tiers trading access speed for price, and rules that move or delete objects between them automatically.

streamablehttp.d: The MCP transport for remote servers, using HTTP POST and GET with optional Server-Sent Events streaming.

stricttooluse.d: A tool-calling mode in which the model's arguments are constrained to match the tool's input schema exactly, so your code can call the function without defensive parsing. Option names differ by provider, so check current docs.

structuraltyping.d: TypeScript's rule that types are compatible when their shapes match, regardless of declared names. It is why two different string IDs are interchangeable unless branded.

structuredconcurrency.d: A design rule that child tasks must finish (or be cancelled) before the block that started them exits, so no task is orphaned and no error is lost. TaskGroup and timeout implement it in asyncio.

structuredoutput.d: Constraining or requesting model output to match a schema such as JSON so code can parse it reliably.

sts.d: The AWS service that issues temporary credentials when a role is assumed.

subagent.d: An agent started by another agent with its own fresh context and often narrower tools. Helps with parallel work, keeping bulky intermediate output out of the main context, and separating privilege (the reader of untrusted pages has no write tools).

subnet.d: A range of IP addresses inside a VPC, tied to one Availability Zone and public or private depending on its routes.

subprocessmod.d: The standard module for running other programs. Pass an argument list (not a shell string), set check=True and a timeout, and avoid shell=True with any user-influenced text to prevent command injection.

subquery.d: A query nested inside another query, used as a value, a list, or a temporary table.

supabase.d: An open-source backend platform built around a Postgres database, adding auto-generated APIs, auth, storage, realtime and edge functions.

supacli.d: Command-line tool that runs the stack locally, manages migrations and deploys functions.

supertest.d: A library for testing HTTP servers by sending requests to an Express app and asserting on the responses.

supervised.d: Learning a mapping from inputs to known labels, for classification or regression.

suspense.d: A React component that shows a fallback while a child loads, enabling streaming of slow parts of a page.

symlink.d: A small file that points at another path (ln -s target link; shown as link -> target by ls -l). Reads and writes follow the link; deleting the link does not delete the target, and a link to a deleted target is broken.

syncwave.d: Argo CD annotations that order a sync: lower waves apply first and must be healthy before the next, and hooks such as PreSync run Jobs like migrations. Flux achieves ordering with dependsOn instead.

syscall.d: The controlled entry from user mode into the kernel for privileged work: open, read, write, fork, mmap, epoll_wait. Each costs hundreds of nanoseconds to microseconds, so programs batch I/O. strace shows a process's system calls.

systemd.d: The init system and service manager on most Linux distributions. Unit files define services and timers; systemctl starts, stops and enables them, and journalctl reads their logs. Restart policies and sandboxing options make it the standard way to run a daemon.

systemprompt.d: Instructions that set a model's role, rules and output format for a whole conversation.

tanstackquery.d: A library that manages server state in the client: caching, request deduplication, retries, background refetching and invalidation. It replaces hand-rolled fetch effects.

targetframework.d: The .NET version a project builds for. .NET 10 is the current LTS, released 11 Nov 2025 and supported to 14 Nov 2028; .NET 8 and 9 reach end of support on 10 Nov 2026. Check the support policy page.

taskgroup.d: An asyncio context manager (3.11+) that owns its child tasks: it waits for all of them, cancels the rest when one fails, and raises an ExceptionGroup. Python 3.15 adds cancel() to stop a group early.

tcp.d: The reliable, ordered transport protocol under HTTP and most databases. Opens with a three-way handshake and retransmits lost packets.

tdd.d: A loop of writing a failing test, writing the least code to pass, then refactoring with the test as a safety net. Strong for well-specified logic and bug fixes, and it nudges designs toward small, injectable units.

temperature.d: A setting that scales token probabilities before sampling: lower is more deterministic, higher is more varied.

tenancy.d: Serving many customers from one system while keeping their data separate, often with a tenant_id column.

tensor.d: An n-dimensional array (scalar, vector, matrix and beyond) that can live on a CPU or GPU. In PyTorch it also records the operations that produced it so gradients can be computed. Tracking tensor shapes catches most deep learning bugs.

tensorparallel.d: Splitting each layer's weight matrices across several GPUs so a model or its KV cache that does not fit on one GPU can be served. It adds inter-GPU communication, so it needs fast links such as NVLink.

terraform.d: HashiCorp's (now IBM's) declarative IaC tool: you describe desired resources in HCL and it plans and applies the changes through provider plugins.

testcontainers.d: A library that starts throwaway real services (Postgres, Redis, Kafka) in Docker for a test run, so integration tests exercise the real engine instead of a lookalike such as SQLite standing in for Postgres.

testdouble.d: A stand-in for a collaborator in a test: dummy (unused filler), stub (canned answers), fake (simplified working version such as an in-memory store), spy (records calls), mock (verifies expected calls). Prefer fakes and real components over heavy mocking.

testpyramid.d: A heuristic: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, a few end-to-end tests. The testing trophy variant puts more weight on integration tests. Both say: test behavior and push each check to the cheapest level that can catch it.

textutils.d: The core text-processing tools: grep filters lines by pattern, awk works on columns, sed edits streams, sort and uniq -c count, xargs builds commands from input, and jq queries JSON. Chained with pipes they answer most log and data questions.

tfbackend.d: Where Terraform or OpenTofu stores state remotely (S3, Azure Storage, HCP Terraform) with locking so two applies cannot run at once. Enable versioning and encryption, and restrict read access because state can contain secrets.

tfimport.d: A configuration block that adopts an existing cloud resource into Terraform state so it can be managed as code, planned and reviewed like any other.

tfmodule.d: A reusable folder of Terraform resources with inputs and outputs. The folder you run commands in is the root module.

tfmoved.d: Declarative blocks for changing infrastructure code without destroying real resources: moved renames or relocates an address, import adopts an existing resource into state, removed drops it from state without deleting it. They go through code review and plan, unlike manual state commands.

tfplan.d: Computes the difference between code, state and the real cloud and shows what apply would create, change or destroy. Review it, especially replacements.

tfprovider.d: A plugin that translates resources into API calls for a platform such as AWS, Azure, Cloudflare or GitHub. Versions are pinned in the lock file.

tfstate.d: The JSON record mapping your resource addresses to real cloud IDs and attributes. Store it remotely, encrypted and locked, because it can contain secrets.

tfworkspace.d: CLI workspaces give one configuration several state files, but they make it easy to apply to the wrong environment. Many teams use a directory or pipeline per environment that calls shared modules, so each environment has its own backend and review.

thinevent.d: A fat event carries the full resource state; a thin event carries only ids and the receiver fetches current state. Thin events stay fresh under reordering and leak less, at the cost of an extra API call.

thread.d: An independent flow of execution inside a process, sharing its memory but with its own stack. Cheap to create and communicate between, but shared memory needs synchronization. In Python the GIL limits CPU-bound parallelism across threads.

threatmodel.d: Structured thinking about what can go wrong with a design before building it: draw data flows, list assets and attackers, and decide controls. STRIDE is a checklist of six threat types (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege).

timesplit.d: Validating by training on the past and testing on the next period (walk-forward), or by keeping every entity entirely on one side of the split (group k-fold). Random splits on time-ordered or repeated-entity data leak information and overstate performance.

timestamptz.d: The Postgres timestamp type that stores an absolute moment in time. Prefer it over timestamp without time zone.

tls.d: The protocol that encrypts and authenticates network connections, behind HTTPS. Use version 1.2 as a minimum, prefer 1.3, and automate certificate renewal.

tls13.d: TLS 1.3 completes in one round trip (zero when resumed with 0-RTT, which has replay risks): client and server exchange key shares, the server presents its certificate, and ephemeral Diffie-Hellman gives forward secrecy. SNI names the host so one IP can serve many certificates.

toil.d: Manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that scales with service size and produces no lasting value. SRE aims to keep it a minority of time.

tokenbucket.d: A rate-limiting algorithm: a bucket holds up to a capacity of tokens and refills at a fixed rate; each request spends one. It allows short bursts but caps the long-run average. Across many servers the state lives in a shared store such as Redis.

tokencost.d: Cost = input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price per call. Long chats multiply input cost; control it with trimmed history, prompt caching for stable prefixes, smaller models and lower max_tokens.

tokenusage.d: Counts returned with every response: input and output tokens, the two billed quantities. Chat history is re-sent each call, so input tokens grow every turn. Log usage per call.

toml.d: Explicitly typed configuration format with [tables], used by pyproject.toml and Cargo. Python reads it with the standard tomllib module (3.11+). Fewer surprises than YAML.

toolcalling.d: A model requesting that your code run a defined function with given arguments, then using the returned result.

toolpoisoning.d: An attack where a malicious tool description or result manipulates the model into harmful actions.

toolresult.d: The user message that answers a tool_use request: one tool_result per tool_use id, containing only those blocks. Extra text after them can cause empty replies or errors; cap the loop's turns.

topp.d: A sampling setting that keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to p.

topsort.d: Ordering the nodes of a directed acyclic graph so every dependency comes before its dependents; it fails if there is a cycle. Used by build systems, package managers, migrations and task schedulers, and it is how circular dependency errors are detected.

torchcompile.d: PyTorch 2's one-line compiler that captures a model and generates fused, optimized kernels. It can give large speedups for little code, at the cost of compile time and occasional graph breaks to debug; measure before and after.

tothread.d: Runs a blocking function in a worker thread and awaits its result, keeping the event loop free. Helps with blocking I/O, not with CPU-bound work because of the GIL.

totp.d: A six-digit code generated by an authenticator app from a shared secret and the current time, valid for about 30 seconds. A decent second factor, but a phishing page can still collect and relay it.

traceback.d: The chain of function calls that led to an error. Read the last line first (what happened), then the frame above it (where it failed), then upward to your own code (how you got there).

traceeval.d: Grading the steps of a run, not just the final text: retrieval recall for RAG, tool choice, step count, repeated failures and respected approval gates for agents. A correct answer reached by an unsafe path is still a failure.

tracing.d: Recording the path of one request through services and steps, with timings, to find where time or errors occur.

trainingskew.d: A mismatch between how features are computed in training and in production, which hurts live accuracy.

transaction.d: A group of statements that succeed or fail together and are isolated from other sessions.

transformer.d: The neural network architecture behind modern LLMs, built from stacked attention and feed-forward layers.

translationinvariance.d: The same shape being recognised wherever it appears. Pixel models lack it (a one-pixel shift dropped accuracy from 0.97 to 0.40 in the lesson); convolution with weight sharing and pooling give some, augmentation adds more.

trie.d: A tree that stores strings by shared prefixes, giving insert and prefix lookup in O(length of the string). The structure behind autocomplete, prefix search and some routers and dictionaries.

trunkbased.d: A workflow where developers merge small changes to main at least daily, hiding unfinished work behind feature flags. It reduces merge pain and supports frequent deploys.

trustedpublishing.d: Letting a package registry accept releases only from a named CI workflow via OIDC, removing long-lived publish tokens that attackers steal. npm and PyPI support it.

trustproxy.d: An Express setting that tells it to trust X-Forwarded headers, so the real client IP is used behind a load balancer.

truthiness.d: Python treats 0, 0.0, empty strings and empty collections, and None as false in conditions; nearly everything else is true. So if items: means "if not empty", and None is tested with is None.

tsgo.d: The Go-based native TypeScript compiler (the project nicknamed Corsa), shipped as TypeScript 7.0 and reported to cut full builds roughly 8x to 12x on large projects. Nightlies ship as @typescript/native-preview.

tsstrict.d: The strict family of compiler options. strict enables the core checks, and noUncheckedIndexedAccess makes array and record lookups possibly undefined.

tsunknown.d: The safe top type: a value could be anything and must be narrowed or validated before use. any, by contrast, switches type checking off and spreads.

tsvector.d: Search built into Postgres: tsvector holds normalized terms, tsquery (plainto_ or websearch_to_tsquery) expresses queries, GIN indexes make them fast and ts_rank orders results. pg_trigram adds typo tolerance. Often enough before adding a dedicated search engine.

ttft.d: How long a request waits before the first output token arrives (queueing plus prefill). Paired with inter-token latency (TPOT), the gap between streamed tokens, it defines how responsive an LLM feels.

ttl.d: Time to live: an expiry set on a key (EXPIRE, or SET with EX) after which Redis deletes it. Every cache and session key should have one, ideally with random jitter so many keys do not expire at the same instant.

turbopack.d: The Rust-based bundler that is the default in Next.js 16 for fast builds and refresh.

twopointers.d: Two techniques that avoid nested loops over sequences. Two pointers move toward each other or in step on sorted data; a sliding window grows on the right and shrinks on the left while maintaining running state. Each element is touched a bounded number of times, giving O(n).

twoscomplement.d: How hardware stores signed integers: the top bit has negative weight, so an 8-bit signed value ranges from -128 to 127 and 11111111 is -1. Fixed-width arithmetic wraps on overflow, causing bugs such as the Year 2038 problem and overflow-based vulnerabilities.

twotower.d: A retrieval architecture with one network encoding the user (and context) and another encoding the item into the same embedding space, with relevance as their dot product. Item vectors are precomputed and served from an ANN index, making it a standard candidate-generation model.

typeddict.d: A dictionary type with known string keys and per-key value types, for JSON-like data. Checked statically; at run time it is a plain dict and validates nothing.

typedresults.d: Helpers like TypedResults.Ok, NotFound, Created and NoContent that return precise results; declaring Results<Ok<Note>, NotFound> puts the possible responses in the method type, which feeds OpenAPI and tests.

typeerasure.d: The fact that TypeScript types disappear at compile time. Anything entering the program at runtime (JSON, env vars, network data) is unchecked until you validate it.

typescript.d: A typed superset of JavaScript whose compiler checks types statically and then erases them, emitting plain JavaScript. TypeScript 7.0 moved the compiler to a native Go implementation.

typevar.d: A placeholder that links types together, such as 'returns the same type it was given'. Python 3.12 writes it as def first[T](items: Sequence[T]) -> T; older code uses TypeVar('T').

unboundedconsumption.d: OWASP LLM10: abuse or missing limits that exhaust cost, latency or capacity, such as a public chatbot run up by bots. Cap tokens, steps and requests per user.

unhandledrejection.d: A promise that rejects with no handler attached. Node.js (since v15) prints the error and exits with status 1; browsers fire an unhandledrejection event. Always await, return or .catch every promise.

unionfind.d: A disjoint-set structure that tracks which items are connected under merges, with near-constant time per operation using path compression and union by rank. Used for Kruskal's spanning tree, grouping equivalent items and connectivity checks.

unitcost.d: Cloud cost divided by a business unit such as requests, active users, orders or inferences. It separates healthy growth (bill up, unit cost down) from waste.

unpacking.d: Assigning parts of a sequence to names: a, b = b, a; first, *rest = items. In calls and literals, * spreads a sequence and ** merges dicts ({**defaults, **overrides}).

unsupervised.d: Finding structure in unlabeled data, such as clusters, patterns or anomalies.

updatetag.d: Next.js APIs for invalidating cached data by label: updateTag expires immediately in Server Actions; revalidateTag refreshes in the background.

upsert.d: Insert a row or update it if it already exists, in one atomic statement: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE in PostgreSQL and SQLite, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE in MySQL.

urlhosttrick.d: A URL whose text starts with a trusted host can still point elsewhere: in https://images.example.com@evil.test the part before @ is a username. Parse the URL and compare the exact hostname, never use startswith.

urlparts.d: https://host:443/notes/2?limit=1#top: scheme (how), host and port (where), path (which resource), query string (filters, key=value joined by &) and a fragment that the browser keeps and never sends to the server.

useactionstate.d: React 19's hook for form actions: it returns the latest result, a form action and a pending flag, so forms need no manual submitting state.

usecache.d: A Next.js 16 directive that opts a page, component or function into caching; part of Cache Components.

useeffect.d: The React hook for synchronizing a component with an external system after render. It re-runs when its dependencies change, and its cleanup runs before the next run and on unmount.

usestate.d: The React hook that gives a component a piece of state and a setter. The value is a snapshot for each render, so use the updater form when the next value depends on the previous one.

usingclause.d: USING filters rows that already exist; WITH CHECK validates rows being inserted or updated.

utf8.d: Unicode assigns each character a code point; UTF-8 encodes code points in 1 to 4 bytes and is the standard on the web. Bytes and text are different types, length depends on what you count, and normalization (NFC) is needed to compare visually identical strings.

uuid.d: A 128-bit identifier that can be generated anywhere without coordination, often used as a primary key.

uvtool.d: A fast Python package and project manager written in Rust that replaces pip, venv, pip-tools, pipx and pyenv. Typical commands: uv init, uv add, uv run, uv sync --locked; it writes a uv.lock lockfile to commit.

vacuum.d: The Postgres process that removes dead row versions and frees their space for reuse.

valkey.d: A BSD-licensed fork of Redis 7.2.4 hosted by the Linux Foundation after Redis changed its license in 2024, backed by large cloud vendors. It is protocol and command compatible with Redis for most uses; newer features and modules diverge between the two.

valueref.d: Whether assignment and function calls copy data or share it. Primitives behave like copies; collections and objects are shared references, so b = a makes two names for one list. Use copy or deepcopy when you need independence.

vectorization.d: Writing an operation for a whole array or column at once (a * 10, df['a'] + df['b']) instead of looping over elements. Faster and shorter; the default style in NumPy and pandas.

venv.d: A per-project folder with its own interpreter link and site-packages so packages for one project do not affect another or the system Python. It is disposable: delete it and rebuild from the lockfile.

vercel.d: A platform that builds and hosts web apps from Git, with a global CDN, preview deployments and on-demand compute.

vfunctions.d: On-demand server code on Vercel that runs route handlers, Server Components and API routes without managing servers.

virtualmemory.d: Each process sees its own address space, which the MMU maps to physical RAM in pages (commonly 4 KB). It gives isolation, lazy allocation, memory-mapped files and copy-on-write. Minor page faults cost about a microsecond; major faults from disk or swap cost milliseconds.

visibilitytimeout.d: In SQS, the period after a message is received during which it is hidden from other consumers. If the consumer does not delete it before the timeout ends, it reappears and is redelivered, so set it above worst-case processing time and extend it for long jobs.

vllm.d: An open-source LLM inference and serving engine from UC Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab built on PagedAttention and continuous batching, with an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server started by vllm serve.

vnetaz.d: Azure's private network, divided into subnets, where you control routing and traffic rules.

vpc.d: A logically isolated network in the cloud where you define IP ranges, subnets, routing and firewalls.

vpcendpoint.d: A private connection from a VPC to an AWS service, avoiding the public internet and NAT charges.

watermark.d: In incremental loads, the high-watermark is the largest timestamp or id already processed, used to fetch only newer rows (with a small overlap for late commits). In streaming, an event-time watermark decides how long to wait for late events before closing a window.

webappfactory.d: Starts the whole ASP.NET Core app in memory and gives a test HttpClient, so tests cover routing, DI, middleware and JSON without a network. Expose Program with 'public partial class Program { }' and override services per test.

webauthn.d: The W3C browser API and protocol behind passkeys and security keys: the server sends a challenge, the authenticator signs it, and the server verifies with the stored public key.

webhook.d: An HTTP request one system sends to another when an event happens. Always verify its signature before acting.

webhooksig.d: Authenticating a webhook by recomputing the HMAC over the exact raw request bytes and comparing in constant time. Parsing and re-serializing the body first breaks the match.

webhookssrf.d: The risk that a webhook sender, which calls customer-supplied URLs, is used to reach internal services or cloud metadata. Block private, loopback and link-local addresses after DNS resolution, limit redirects and run workers in a restricted network.

weightinit.d: Starting values for the weights. All zeros makes every hidden neuron identical forever (loss stuck at ln 2); small random values scaled to the layer size break the symmetry and keep signals a sensible size.

wellarchitected.d: AWS's review framework of six pillars for judging cloud designs: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance, cost and sustainability.

wheel.d: A wheel is a pre-built Python package that installs without compiling; an sdist is source that may need a compiler. New Python releases can lack wheels for compiled libraries for a few weeks, which delays upgrades.

window.d: Computes a value across related rows, such as a rank or running total, without collapsing them like GROUP BY.

workerthreads.d: A Node module for running JavaScript on separate threads, used to keep CPU-heavy work off the main event loop.

workingdir.d: The folder a shell session is currently 'in'. Relative paths and most commands act relative to it; pwd prints it and cd changes it.

xgboost.d: A widely used gradient boosting library with histogram-based trees, strong regularization, GPU and distributed training, and a scikit-learn style API. Key knobs: learning_rate, max_depth, min_child_weight, subsample, colsample_bytree.

xmltags.d: Tag-like markers such as <instructions>, <document> and <question> that separate the parts of a prompt (rules, data, examples, inputs). They are a convention the models follow well, not enforced syntax; use consistent names and refer to them in the instructions. Escape your own closing tags in untrusted text.

xss.d: Injection of attacker JavaScript into a page other users view, letting it act as them or read page data. Prevent with output encoding, framework escaping and a strict Content Security Policy.

yaml.d: Indentation-based, human-friendly format for configuration (Kubernetes, CI pipelines). It guesses types: in YAML 1.1 parsers NO is false and 3.10 is the number 3.1, so quote such values; load with safe_load.

zeroshot.d: Asking a model to do a task with instructions only and no examples. Fine for simple, well-known tasks; add examples (few-shot) when the output format, tone or edge-case handling must be exact.

zod.d: A TypeScript-first schema library for validating and parsing untrusted data, such as request bodies.
